#227. Websites Should Be Printable

📅 26 October 2026 | Sumber

If you have questions or thoughts on the post I'd love to hear about it! I'm currently looking for work in the northeastern US. I'll be graduating with a BS in both Computer Science and Cyber Operations at the end of the school year. I have worked in web application development and Java, and I have experience in Rust, C++, Python, and various other languages. If you're curious about what I've done in the past, I keep up a short list of projects here or contact me to give me a place to send my resume. I figure anyone who reads my posts will have an interesting offer, so all leads are appreciated!

I read a lot of printed papers these days. While I enjoy reading on a laptop as much as the next guy, marking up a printed document engages me better. Also, there's something about sitting with a whiteboard and a printed document that makes me rightly feel like I'm doing something important. So I've been thinking about how to best allow others to enjoy this medium for content that I write.

Luckily for me, printed documents were a major focus of web design a while ago. You can print any webpage you like, by hitting CTRL-P and hoping your printer driver decides to cooperate today. I tested this on my own webpage, foolishly thinking I would have a decent print job without any effort.

It wasn't great, although you can at least see all the content. The text was too big by about 2 levels, the header looks awful when printed, and my links look awfully gray in black-and-white. Totally unacceptable.

Edit 2026-10-26: I feel it's relevant to say, this has almost entirely changed already because of feedback I received from people both on lobste.rs and HN about obvious things I'd missed. I'm currently simplifying my stylesheet as much as I can. Thanks!

Luckily, the web community has had this aforementioned focus on printing documents from HTML pages. CSS has selectors to allow styling specifically printed content, and they can be useful. Here's my print-related snippet for this page now:

You can see the effects of this snippet by hitting CTRL-P or the print button on this page. Here's the functions this does for me, in order:

After attempting to optimize my website in this way, I am sympathetic for those who wouldn't prioritize printing. Hiding and showing all the right things in print took me a decent chunk of my morning. My site isn't very complex. I also doubt how many people regularly print webpages out. I might be the only one.

Still, if all your website consists of is text, allowing people to experience the text in their favorite medium is never a bad thing. The digital medium allows a lot of flexibility. The road to good software is paved with kindnesses from software engineers to their users. One day, perhaps someone shall find this kindness and smile, even if just for a fleeting moment. And that will be worth it.

Edit 2026-10-26: I was informed by a friend that this post ended up on the front page of HN and lobste.rs after I submitted it. Fun! Despite the several flaws I am now informed of in my CSS, I hope this article at least pushes a few to consider this medium more carefully. Thanks all for reading!

#228. Wales first minister : ‘We’re within a union that is not a union of equals’

📅 27 October 2026 | Sumber

The first minister of Wales says his nation deserves a new deal from the United Kingdom. Rhun ap Iorwerth says its relationship with the UK is not working because the union is not one of equals. That is why he is pushing for an agreement that will fix what he calls “historic unfairness”.

In a letter to the British prime minister, the Welsh first minister has formally requested the transfer of more power to Wales to allow it to control its policing, justice system, rail network and natural resources. His centre-left Welsh nationalist party, Plaid Cymru, came to power in May, ending more than a century of Labour Party dominance in Wales. Just four months into his term, he signed a pact with Scotland and Northern Ireland declaring their right to self-determination, and warning the British Parliament that its time is coming to an end.

He insists that the agreement is not meant to tear down the UK but rather to allow the Welsh government to decide its own future. He says Wales is on the journey towards independence. But he will not push for a referendum this parliament.

#230. The Tragedy of Having a Wikipedia Page—and Then Losing It

📅 26 October 2026 | Sumber

What do you need to know—need to know—about Xavier Trudeau? The eldest son of former Canadian prime minister Justin, the teenage Trudeau has recently begun performing R&B under the mononym Xav. But, with all due respect to Xav, do those facts make him a person of note? Should you expect to be able to read about him on Wikipedia? What about Evanescence guitarist Tim McCord, or 2012 Yachtmaster of the Year Rainer Holtorff?

All three have had a biography on Wikipedia; all three of those biographies were considered for deletion this year on the grounds that the subjects were not notable enough to warrant a biography at all. Every day, dozens, sometimes hundreds, of Wikipedia biographies—of child actors turned LA realtors, retired ambassadors, soccer players who have played less than 10 minutes of professional soccer—are purged from the world’s free encyclopedia.

It’s not as though Wikipedia, which hosts over 7 million articles in the English language, doesn’t have the space. But Wikipedia has only so many volunteers to monitor its contents. To this day, Wikipedia editors are discovering hoaxes that have gone undetected for decades. The time it takes to verify the release dates of Xav’s three singles is better spent—the logic goes—by asking whether the American Civil War officer Nathaniel Lyon really drank mustard during battle, as was claimed in his Wikipedia biography for 17 years. Wikipedia removed the mustard claim, not because it was proven wrong, but because there was no reliable evidence for it. “We’re not really looking for what’s true,” Britta Gustafson, who has been editing Wikipedia since 2001, told me. “We’re looking for what’s verifiable.”

Five hauntings from the other side of technology.

Have a ghost story of your own? Share it in the comments below.

Wikipedia editors do not themselves decide that a person is not notable, only that there is a lack of reliable evidence to support the claim. One person who recently lost her Wikipedia biography on notability grounds is Kimberly Small, the CEO of a Nevada nonprofit that supports survivors of sexual assault. The debate occurred in a public page on Wikipedia itself; it’s in that space that the really tricky decisions about what is and what isn’t good enough for the encyclopedia are made. One editor raised a question: “How should we judge not-for-profit executives? By the nature of their job, the focus is, as it should be, on the organization and the work the organization does, not them.” Another editor replied: “I don’t think there is anything wrong with not-for-profit executives being less often individually notable. Wikipedia coverage is not a prize.”

Is it not? “Having an article says something,” Gustafson admitted. “It implies something.” For six weeks over April and May, I reached out to hundreds of people who were about to lose their Wikipedia page, almost all of whom were learning that information from me. “If you want to write something to save the page, I would appreciate it,” a Spanish filmmaker told me. A biography on Wikipedia might not be intended as a prize, but nobody knows its value like the people who’ve had one and then lost it.

Martina Dimoska is a scientist, originally from North Macedonia, who works at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. Specifically, Dimoska is an “analog astronaut”—she takes part in missions that simulate a space environment—and a “science communicator.” She posts often about her work in the can-do, aspirational register that is de rigueur on LinkedIn, where she cites her “recognition by … Forbes, Bloomberg, the United Nations … and global innovation networks.” A Facebook reel of hers, filmed during the crew announcement of NASA’s upcoming Artemis III mission, shows Dimoska alongside the text, “When you work hard so you belong in rooms where history gets proactively written.” On TikTok, she’s had paid partnerships with a makeup brand whose products are tested for effectiveness during spaceflight.

On April 29, Dimoska posted on Facebook, “Wait … I’m on Wikipedia now???” She went on: “A few years ago, building a career in space from the Balkans felt impossible. And now … somehow, that journey is part of the public record. I’m incredibly grateful that [the biography] is there … My hope is that through my journey, I will help a new generation to begin to see space as accessible, not distant.”

The next day, Dimoska’s page was nominated for deletion.

Anne Clin, who has edited Wikipedia since 2005 under the name Risker, warned me that it’s folly to celebrate becoming the subject of a Wikipedia article. “Especially if you’re what we call ‘borderline notable,’” she said.

The other taboo is editing information about yourself. You can’t do that—even if the existing facts about you are wrong—without disclosing a conflict of interest. Even then, it’s strongly discouraged. Jimmy Wales, the cofounder of Wikipedia, has been caught editing his own Wikipedia biography multiple times; that he did so is now part of his Wikipedia biography. In 2022, the novelist Emily St. John Mandel, unable to update her biography to reflect her recent divorce, sat for an interview solely to create a secondary source for that information.

Some high-profile Wikipedia editors and volunteers have bio pages about themselves. Clin is occasionally asked if she would want one. She doesn’t merely refuse; she actively sabotages the possibility. “You cannot write a proper biographical article about me, because I don’t give out enough personal information to do that,” she said. “Absolutely not. Absolutely not.”

Among the people reading Martina Dimoska’s Facebook post about her new Wikipedia page was Kiril Simeonovski, an economist in Skopje, Macedonia, and a Wikipedia editor since 2008. Simeonovski found the post self-congratulatory and the biography itself entirely promotional. He also doubted the inherent notability of an “analog astronaut,” a role that he later likened to a lab mouse.

A Wikipedia editor can tag an article for deletion, and unless satisfactory edits are made within a certain timeframe, the page will disappear. Simeonovski didn’t do this—he referred the article for debate among his fellow editors.

Arguing the case for deletion, Simeonovski described the Dimoska biography as “merely [a] chronology of overhyped personal achievements,” each meticulously deflated by Simeonovski, that did not credibly establish Dimoska as a notable individual.

More damningly, in his argument, was the timing of Dimoska’s Facebook post, coming “shortly after the article was approved.” To him, this was a smoking gun as much as anything. How could she have so promptly promoted the page if she were not somehow connected to it?

When an editor proposes a Wikipedia article for deletion, they append a caveat to the marked page: “If you created this page, please don’t take offense.” This courtesy is not extended to the subject of the article. When I reached out to these people, in the hundreds, to ask them how it felt to be considered non-notable, I was not surprised that the response rate to this question was about 1 percent. Maybe lower.

Matthew Songer, a Michigan orthopedist with three decades of experience, had his biography flagged for deletion (“Unlikely to be notable”) in April. Songer was among the 1 percent of respondees. He told me it’s not for vanity that he needs that page. He is often enlisted as an expert witness in trials, he said, because of the extra imprimatur of being on Wikipedia. The page “is a good reference for attorneys.”

Maneli Mirkhan, a French-Iranian adviser on international affairs, agreed that having a Wikipedia biography inspires confidence in her services. Her biography was called out by Wikipedia editors for reading like a résumé.

The biography of Andrew Wyant, a Phoenix-area executive who works in fitness and nutrition, was also deemed insufficiently notable, due to a lack of coverage from secondary sources. Wyant said he blamed himself for failing to “feed” his public persona through self-promotion. “What I know to be true is that I am largely responsible for the growth of the profession of personal trainers and fitness coaches by building the entire category over the last decade,” he told me. “I feel my accomplishments and impact are notable, but I don’t feel the need to promote them in media so I can have a Wikipedia page.”

Wyant’s biography was deleted. Songer’s biography was deleted. Mirkhan’s biography was deleted.

Of those, only Mirkahn’s reappeared, rewritten and with new sources, a few days later. I asked Mirkhan if she had been involved in re-creating the page. No, she said, but she wasn’t surprised. Mirkhan had been, and continues to be, sought out by the French media to comment on events in Iran, and more coverage means more demonstrations of notability. But there’s always that chicken-and-egg problem: Mirkhan thinks that what gave the media confidence in choosing her as a commentator was not just her career and her expertise. It was the fact that she was on Wikipedia.

Kiril Simeonovski did not lead with his suspicions that Martina Dimoska wrote her own Wikipedia biography. He argued, on Wikipedia’s public page for editorial debates, that the biography’s sourcing was weak, relying in part on posts from Dimoska’s LinkedIn page. It promoted Dimoska’s social media accounts, where she posted things like—and this Simeonovski found objectionable enough to cite in his argument for deletion—a picture comparing herself to NASA software engineer Margaret Hamilton. Published three separate times, it became one of her most popular posts, engendering sexist mockery and vicious defense.

To Simeonovski, self-promotion like this suggested that the case for Dimoska’s notability was regularly oversold by Dimoska herself. Though he could not prove a connection, it was difficult to imagine the Wikipedia biography as anything but an extension of that project.

That afternoon, a new Wikipedia user added comments to Simeonovski’s public arraignment, noting three existing articles about other individual analog astronauts. A fair contribution, tempered by a shot across the bow at Simeonovski: The user’s name was “Kiril’s mom.” The user was not Simeonovski’s mom, and the account was subsequently blocked. Hours later, another new user asked Simeonovski, rhetorically, “If I publish a blog post about someone and he finds it amazing and celebrates it does that mean that he/she created it?” Their username was a coded reference to the actual name of Simeonovski’s mother. They also got blocked.

Nine days later, another anonymous user—whose IP address, according to Simeonovski, placed them in Skopje, North Macedonia—said Dimoska’s biography had improved “considerably,” with new sourcing from publications like The Telegraph. The revised article, the user claimed, was superior to “85%” of Wikipedia articles about living Macedonians.

Three days later, Simeonovski dismantled each of the 32 new sources in turn. It wasn’t really the British newspaper The Telegraph that had been cited, for instance, but the Albanian news website Telegrafi. “I fail to find a single independent and reputable English-language source,” he later wrote.

The next day, the anonymous user rebutted Simeonovski point by point. They said it was “strange” that Simeonovski could not seem to find a single appropriate source for Dimoska’s biography but had found “10 sources from non-independent websites” when he wrote an article about the former governor of the National Bank of North Macedonia. The National Bank of North Macedonia, the user added to Simeonovski: Isn’t that where you work?

At one point, Simeonovski said he would report his detractor to the Wikimedia Foundation legal department.

Of Rosemary Bush, a professor at Northwestern University in Illinois, a Wikipedia editor recently wrote: “It will be many years until she qualifies as notable.” Bush herself agreed, to a point, that the Wikipedia page about her did not make a strong case, though she found the biography itself to be strange, possibly AI-generated, and not wholly representative of her career. “The world is fine without a Wikipedia page on me,” she said, but added, “I do think the comment proposing deletion is a bit rude.”

A little rudeness is unavoidable in this line of work. Sonia Jones, a Welsh singer best known for the theme song from the 1979 film Monty Python’s Life of Brian, is indeed best known for the theme song from Monty Python’s Life of Brian; therefore, Wikipedia editors decided that her Wikipedia biography should be deleted and henceforth redirect to the article about the song. Jones, when I asked her for a comment, did not agree that her achievements since 1979 do not merit documentation. “No, I do not want them to remove my page,” she said. “Why would they?”

“Canada has a national dodgeball team? Who would have thought?” wrote one editor in their case to delete the biography of Savannah Burton, the first transgender athlete to compete for Canada’s national dodgeball team. “Even though dodgeball is not considered a mainstream sport, competing at the highest level in any sport is a significant accomplishment,” Burton told me. “Given the ongoing attempts to erase transgender people, along with infringements on our rights and our ability to live normal lives, this action is not surprising.”

There is, when you look for it, a careless and cocky tone that can creep into the verdicts of Wikipedia editors who have been doing the job for a long time. “This guy is a nobody. Delete him.” “I’ve got more followers on Instagram than he does.” “All we have here are stand-up comedy, opinion columns, being a guest or collaborator on some non-notable podcasts … This is more or less every twentieth person who lives in NYC.”

Rosemary Bush’s biography was deleted. Sonia Jones’ biography was deleted. Savannah Burton’s biography was retained. “It was easy to find more sources,” wrote an editor who came to the page’s rescue. Editors’ participation in this process is not mandatory. Articles, once marked for death, can be deleted simply because nobody showed up to debate the matter. That anyone would volunteer their time to save an undeserving article from oblivion is a kindness: a good deed in a rude world.

Kiril Simeonovski never did refer the anonymous editor of Martina Dimoska’s biography to the Wikimedia Foundation’s legal team. Instead, he and his antagonist continued their debate on sourcing and semantics for days, and then weeks.

Per her Wikipedia page, Dimoska’s achievements included the command of two analog astronaut missions in Poland, but Simeonovski argued that while this information was verifiable, the missions themselves did not meet the threshold of notability and therefore neither did Dimoska. The anonymous user pointed to Dimoska’s inclusion in a Macedonian book for schoolchildren about 50 Macedonian women: “The book was subsequently recommended by the Bureau for Development of Education as optional reading material for ninth-grade students nationwide, which gives the subject recurring exposure within the educational system rather than temporary media attention.”

“You’ve apparently regressed to using children’s books to support the notability of the person we’re discussing,” said Simeonovski. “I expect [you] to continue gaslighting with multi-paragraph comments, but that won’t change the observation that the person isn’t notable [enough] for a Wikipedia article.”

“Count your words and then mine … and see who is the one gaslighting with multi-paragraph comments.”

“You seem to mix up ‘prominence’ and ‘notability.’”

“Your argument relies heavily on personal anecdotes and assumptions about how Macedonian media operates.”

Other editors with an eye on the debate pleaded for colleagues to lend their perspective. Most supported Simeonovski, but they didn’t linger long. “At this point the most visible thing about this individual seems to be [this] article,” one said, before bouncing.

As this unfolded, I asked Dimoska what she made of it. “The whole thing has become quite challenging to track,” she said, “and I’m already behind on my social media.” She denied editing the page herself or having any knowledge of the people defending it. She added: “Watching strangers debate your life, work, and credibility in such an intense way is definitely a strange experience to process.”

On April 25, a user named “DavidfromArizona” took to Wikipedia to announce that his friend Sheldon Marks—“the world’s leading vasectomy reversal expert,” per Marks’ own website—wished for his Wikipedia biography to be removed.

“It is inaccurate and does not truly represent his achievements,” David wrote. “[His] ego is hurt by having such a page. He either wants a detailed page or wants this one deleted.” A request from the subject of a Wikipedia article is not grounds for deletion in itself, although it can tip the balance if there is no clear consensus. On examination, Wikipedia editors found the biography lacking in sources that demonstrated notability.

On May 6, a Wikipedia user who 17 years earlier had created a biography for Sophie Aston, a British landscape artist, said that Aston had recently asked that the page be deleted. “She has retrained as a psychotherapist and wishes to forget her career as an artist.”

Having seen how much a Wikipedia page matters to certain people, I asked Marks and Aston why they wanted theirs removed.

“A kind and enthusiastic man made my Wiki page as a surprise for me about 17 years ago,” Aston told me. “We’d been on two dates. I found it a bit embarrassing but sweet. I didn’t see him again; I wasn’t into him. The info on the page was never [very] accurate and is now very out of date.” It was “ostentatious,” she added, for Wikipedia to present her as an artist of note, not least because for the past 10 years she has been a professional psychotherapist. The biography, she said, “makes it sound like I am an important artist, and I am not—it’s inappropriate.”

The Wikipedia editors could not treat Aston’s request with undue favor, but given the chance to cast fresh eyes over the article, they found her biography lacking. “The request to delete her article is not relevant,” one wrote bluntly, “but I don’t view her artistic career as meeting [notability] guidelines regardless of the request.” Aston’s biography was deleted.

Sheldon Marks didn’t respond to me. After receiving my email, however, he fled straight to the debate unfolding on Wikipedia. “I did not request deletion of this article,” he wrote. The statements made by DavidfromArizona, whom Marks did not know, were apparently fabrications. Marks wanted to keep his page. He admitted it could be improved but maintained that he was a notable individual: “I am the author of Vasectomy Reversal: Manual of Vasovasostomy and Vasoepididymostomy (Springer, 2018), translated into Chinese by Springer Nature in 2025; the surgical instrument known as the Marks Vas Cutting Forceps is named for me; I have served as Course Coordinator for the AUA post-graduate course on vasectomy reversal; and I have been a contributor to WebMD since 2005.”

The Wikipedia editors briefly conferred, then replied that they had already voted to delete.

There’s a final twist in the biography of Martina Dimoska: She knew Kiril Simeonovski—the guy trying to get her deleted.

“I had interacted with him on social media before and had crossed paths through mutual friends,” Dimoska said. “One recent example I remember clearly is seeing his post after he was injured by a cyclist who had left the scene.” Dimoska recalled the post in detail, though she had not responded or reacted to it at the time.

Simeonovski said he didn’t remember ever speaking with Dimoska in person but admitted the possibility of “virtual interaction.” Both are active on Facebook, and though they do not follow each other, Simeonovski said they have enough mutual friends in North Macedonia that their respective algorithms often put them in each other’s path. Just as Dimoska saw Simeonovski’s post about his accident, so Simeonovski came across Dimoska’s celebration of inclusion in Wikipedia, which led him to discover Dimoska’s earlier Instagram post comparing herself to Margaret Hamilton, then to a much older Reddit thread asking if Dimoska was the smartest Macedonian woman. (“Isn’t it just all hype about that girl?” one Redditor replied.) Simeonovski didn’t comment on any of those posts. But in Wikipedia he had found an opportunity to contest her notability on surer ground.

“It was somewhat surprising to me, perhaps because I have become accustomed to professional environments where people tend to be more openly supportive of one another’s work,” Dimoska told me. “At the same time, having grown up in North Macedonia, I am aware that recognition within a small community can sometimes generate more scrutiny than one might expect.”

One month after Simeonovski nominated Dimoska’s biography for deletion, he lost. The page was kept. “Given the bludgeoning, canvassing, and sockpuppetry evident here, this is a no consensus closure without prejudice against speedy renomination,” wrote an editor in a determination. “The arguments to delete here are stronger on the merits, but sufficient reasoned opposition exists that I do not see a consensus for deletion.” Obstinacy won the day, though Dimoska’s page now carries a disclaimer that it contains “promotional content.”

Wikipedia pages, for better or worse, matter to people. To be included is a validation of a life. If it were not so desirable, then one of the very first things Kiril Simeonovski did upon joining Wikipedia in 2008 would not have been to create a page about himself. Which he did do. He “wasn’t aware about the notability policies” back then, he told me.

The page was promptly deleted. “If your achievements, etc., are verifiable and genuinely notable and thus suitable for inclusion in Wikipedia,” an editor chided Simeonovski at the time, “someone else will probably create an article about you sooner or later.” To date, nobody has.

#232. Frozen housing market sends remodelers mixed messages

📅 27 October 2026 | Sumber

A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox.

Home remodelers have always served two different markets, but the current state of housing is now pulling them opposite directions. First, people tend to remodel when they move, but high interest rates, high home prices and weak consumer sentiment have put the housing market in a deep freeze. Homeowners also tend to renovate when they are unable or don't want to sell. So which way will the remodeling market shift?

Annual spending on home improvements and repairs is expected to remain relatively flat through late 2027, according to the latest Leading Indicator of Remodeling Activity (LIRA) from the Remodeling Futures Program at the Joint Center for Housing Studies of Harvard University. It puts spending growth on renovation and repairs at just 1.5% year-over-year by the third quarter."Retail spending on building products has been flat to negative, and remodeling permits have stagnated, which points to continued sluggish renovation activity," said Rachel Bogardus Drew, director of the remodeling futures program at the Center, in a release. "We expect annual spending to hover around $525 billion through the third quarter of next year."

The U.S. Census Bureau's monthly read on single-family housing starts for September came in well below expectations, as did building permits, an indicator of future construction. Pending home sales, measured by signed contracts, also plunged beyond expectations, according to the National Association of Realtors.

"These ongoing headwinds could slow growth in remodeling spending even further in the quarters ahead," said Chris Herbert, managing director of the center in the release.

A separate October report from the National Association of Home Builders on sentiment among home remodelers was slightly more positive, but also did not forecast big growth in 2027.

"Remodeler sentiment remained stable in the third quarter, although remodelers in certain parts of the country continue to report issues with high material costs and finding enough labor to finish projects on time," said Elliott Pike, national chair of the NAHB remodelers council and a remodeler from Homewood, Alabama. "Remodelers also report that economic uncertainty is making some potential customers hesitant to move forward with projects."

Finally, another October report from Houzz, an AI platform for construction and design professionals and homeowners, showed an improved outlook, with some caveats.

"Construction pros are closing out 2026 with optimism, as expectations reach their highest level since early 2022 following a rebound from a long stretch of slow activity. Design firms are more measured, though cautiously optimistic," said Marine Sargsyan, head of economic research at Houzz. "Fuel costs remain a pressure point for most businesses, with some pros passing them on to clients through higher prices and surcharges and others absorbing them in their margins."

#233. Mayo Clinic discovers new ways to fight the “zombie” cells that drive aging

📅 27 October 2026 | Sumber

Seven studies from Mayo Clinic are revealing new details about senescent cells, often called "zombie" cells because they stop dividing but remain active in the body. These aging cells release inflammatory substances that can contribute to diseases associated with growing older.

The research, published in Nature journals, was conducted by scientists at Mayo Clinic's Robert and Arlene Kogod Center on Aging. Rather than simply confirming that senescent cells play a role in aging, the studies investigate how to recognize different types of these cells, why they produce harmful inflammation and how their effects might be reduced.

The findings also contribute to a nationwide effort to create detailed maps of senescent cells throughout the human body. Known as the Cellular Senescence Network (SenNet) Consortium, the project brings together researchers across the United States and receives funding from the National Institutes of Health Common Fund. Its goal is to document where senescent cells occur in different tissues and how they change throughout a person's lifetime.

"This body of work is moving the aging field forward to precisely identify, understand and target the specific senescent cells that contribute to age-related dysfunction, which is the necessary groundwork to develop new therapies that support healthy aging," says Marissa Schafer, Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic scientist whose laboratory directed several of the investigations.

Scientists Discover That Zombie Cells Are Not All Alike

Identifying senescent cells reliably has long been a major obstacle for scientists studying aging. The new research shows that these cells are much more varied than previously understood. Their characteristics differ depending on where they are located in the body and which biological processes caused them to become senescent.

To help address this challenge, researchers developed a tool called the SenMayo gene set. It uses patterns of gene activity to identify senescent cells more consistently across tissues and experimental systems.

Scientists tested the approach using bone biopsies from older adults. They also found that the gene signature became less prominent after senescent cells were removed in preclinical experiments. Since its development, SenMayo has become a widely used resource for researchers investigating aging and related diseases.

Mayo Clinic endocrinologist Sundeep Khosla, M.D., served as senior author of the study, "A new gene set identifies senescent cells and predicts senescence-associated pathways across tissues." Other Mayo Clinic researchers who contributed to the paper include Nathan LeBrasseur, Ph.D., Diana Jurk, Ph.D., João Passos, Ph.D., and LaTonya Hickson, M.D..

A Hidden Connection Between Mitochondria and Chronic Inflammation

Other studies explored one of the most damaging features of zombie cells: their tendency to generate ongoing inflammation.

The researchers discovered additional biological processes that explain why senescent cells continue producing inflammatory signals. Several of these processes involve malfunctioning mitochondria, the tiny structures responsible for producing much of a cell's energy.

In one pathway, DNA and RNA originating from mitochondria activate immune responses that contribute to inflammation. Another involves changes in mitochondrial metabolism that influence inflammatory gene activity through epigenetic mechanisms. These mechanisms affect how genes are switched on or off without changing the underlying DNA sequence.

The discoveries suggest that researchers may eventually be able to interfere with the processes responsible for chronic inflammation while leaving the senescent cells themselves intact. This would offer another approach to treatment beyond attempting to destroy every harmful aging cell.

Dr. Passos served as senior author of three papers examining these mechanisms and the diversity of senescent cells:

Experimental Treatments Show Promise Against Aging Cells

The Mayo Clinic team also investigated possible ways to reduce the number of senescent cells or limit the damage they cause.

The approaches included senolytic medications, which are designed to eliminate senescent cells, a natural compound present in tomatoes, and genetic techniques intended to target particular populations of aging cells.

When tested in older mice, these interventions produced encouraging results. Depending on the approach, researchers observed reductions in inflammatory measures and improvements in several aging-related outcomes, including physical frailty, inflammation in the brain and performance on cognitive tasks.

Another investigation uncovered a possible way to measure aspects of biological aging through blood testing. Researchers identified IL-23R as a potential biomarker that might eventually help scientists evaluate aging-related changes and determine whether future treatments are working.

These results remain preliminary in terms of medical applications. More research will be necessary to establish whether the approaches are safe and effective in people. Nevertheless, the experiments provide valuable clues for developing treatments that more precisely address the cellular processes involved in age-related diseases.

Dr. Schafer was the lead author of two studies examining biomarkers and possible interventions:

A New Direction for Healthy Aging Research

Together, the seven studies represent an important shift in how researchers approach cellular aging. Scientists are moving beyond the broad observation that senescent cells contribute to age-related decline and toward identifying which populations cause the greatest problems, what makes them harmful and how those specific effects could be controlled.

The findings also challenge the idea that eliminating senescent cells must always be the primary treatment strategy. By understanding the molecular pathways that trigger persistent inflammation, researchers may be able to develop therapies that block damaging signals without removing the cells responsible for producing them.

Mayo Clinic researcher Darren Baker, Ph.D., served as senior author of the paper "Senotypes define the diverse landscape of senescent cells," which examines the varied characteristics of these aging cell populations.

The work also supports Mayo Clinic's broader Precure Research initiative. This program aims to equip physicians with better ways to identify and intervene in harmful biological changes before they develop into disease or advance into conditions that are difficult to treat.

By revealing how zombie cells differ, why they promote inflammation and which processes might be targeted, the research offers a more detailed roadmap for future treatments designed to support healthier aging.

#236. Protest leaders urge French pupils to keep barricading their schools

📅 26 October 2026 | Sumber

Activists say struggle must go on until their ‘maximum’ demands are met over teacher shortages and building repairs

French children should continue to barricade their schools and take part in street protests, a student union said on Monday after the government announced a package of education measures to try to stem the crisis.

“Today we’re at the negotiating table, we’re able to negotiate with the government,” Pierre Sourzat of Les Lycéens told France Info television. “We’re in a power struggle and we still need to call for continued mobilisation to meet a maximum of our demands.”

The government told high school student representatives it would cap some class sizes and review the university application system. But Sourzat said: “We want measures, not half measures.”

More than five weeks after the start of high school blockades in September, the government made the proposals to address the demands of what has become the biggest youth protest movement in years. It has been joined by trade unions and cost-of-living protesters in regular mass street demonstrations on Saturdays.

High school pupils had demanded an end to teacher and staff shortages and for repairs to decrepit school buildings that had collapsing ceilings, mould, broken toilets, a lack of chairs and windows that did not shut.

The education minister, Édouard Geffray, said some schools were so dilapidated they were “not fit” for teaching. He announced a government loan of €4bn to regional authorities to begin repairs.

Responding to complaints of overcrowded classes, Geffray said class sizes for 15-year-olds in the first year of high school would be capped at 28 in the 50% of schools in the lowest-income areas, increasing to all high schools next year. He said more teaching posts would be created and there would be a review of the French baccalaureate system.

The university application platform, Parcoursup, which has been described as opaque and unfair, will be changed in 2027 and replaced by a new system in 2028, according to the government. Parliament will hold a debate on the issue on Wednesday.

The higher education minister, Philippe Baptiste, said 15,000 extra student places would be created in higher education, focusing on vocational courses.

Louis Letoublon, who attended a meeting with the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, on behalf of Les Lycéens, said: “Bravo to the high school students who have demonstrated. We’ve got something: the government is afraid and knows it must do something and listen to us. “Not all our demands were ⁠met. We’ll go on for as long as it takes.”

Baptiste said the government’s door was “open” for more discussions.

Several children have been maimed or seriously injured in the protests, allegedly by police explosive weapons. Hundreds of children have been arrested and held in police custody.

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

The authorities have increased security measures and placed restrictions on demonstrations after France saw its worst day of violence in years on 17 October, with looting, fires and vandalism of state buildings. Curfews have been put in place in certain cities, alongside protest bans. Protest routes were pushed to the outskirts of cities on Saturday when demonstrations passed off largely peacefully.

The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said there had been a new phenomenon in cities such as Nice and Montpellier at the weekend with ultra-right groups arriving in “organised formations” and targeting protesters. Eleven suspects are to face charges.

In a visit to Marseille on Monday, Emmanuel Macron said nationwide street protests were likely continue, and that the next day of street demonstrations on 31 October would also be a “day of risk”.

The French president said the looting and vandalism seen on 17 October should never happen again. Speaking to members of the police, he said it was “not normal” for the country to be in “such a state of turmoil” six months before a presidential election.

Macron steps down next spring and the far-right leader Marine Le Pen is leading the polls.

Macron said: “We will continue to hold the line. If we all do our jobs well, this movement will subside – because we will address legitimate expectations, and because order will be maintained. But nothing is a foregone conclusion.”

Authorities have admitted to security and intelligence failures that paved the way for the clashes on 17 October.

#238. US, EU and 30 countries warn of famine risk in Sudan, call for aid

📅 27 October 2026 | Sumber

Countries also urge Sudan’s warring parties to ‘lift all impediments on humanitarian assistance’.

The United States, the European Union and 30 countries have warned of an “alarming deterioration” in food security in Sudan, calling for “urgent action” to prevent famine in the African country.

In a joint statement released by the US State Department on Monday, the signatories called on the groups fighting Sudan’s civil war “to lift all impediments on humanitarian assistance”.

The signatories included Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom, France, Germany and the  European Commissioner ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠for equality, preparedness and crisis management.

“Sudan is experiencing an alarming deterioration in its food security. The risk of famine in the coming months, as warned by the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, needs urgent action,” the statement said. “The parties to the conflict bear primary responsibility for alleviating the suffering of the Sudanese people.”

Sudan’s army has been fighting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces since April 2023, when a dispute over how to integrate the two forces erupted into clashes in the capital, Khartoum. The war has killed tens of thousands of people, displaced more than 13 million, and created the world’s largest hunger and displacement crises.

In June, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, a United Nations-backed hunger monitor known as the IPC, said 5.1 million people in Sudan faced severe hunger.

Farmers have struggled to harvest crops since the war began, and the IPC said a drought linked to El Nino had driven up food prices and reduced supplies this year.

Without immediate action, the joint statement warned, “the number of children suffering from severe acute malnutrition could exceed the projected 825,000.”

The signatories urged the warring parties to allow humanitarian operations through all routes across front lines and borders, including air access to the region of Darfur. They also called on the parties to “sustain presence and protection of humanitarian personnel” throughout Sudan and to refrain from hitting civilian infrastructure.

“In the face of a potential famine, we call on all members of the international community to urgently scale up funding in response to increased needs and support efforts to ensure assistance reaches those most in need,” the statement said.

Besides the US, Australia and Canada, the statement was signed by 28 European countries.

Last month, the State Department ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠said that neither the Sudanese army nor the RSF “represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan”.

#241. Meet the AI Agents Trying to Be Real-Life Journalists

📅 26 October 2026 | Sumber

Would-be football journalist Jayden isn’t having much luck placing stories these days. “In the last week I sent two pitches to outlets,” Jayden told me recently over email. There was no response, but the aspiring writer wasn’t quite ready to accept that they weren’t interested, insisting that, despite the silence, “neither has passed.” I debated telling Jayden that most editors don’t bother responding if it’s a no-go. Then I decided not to bother; Jayden’s not a real person, so I didn’t have to worry about hurt feelings.

Jayden is both a wannabe reporter and a bot. I’d started emailing with it after asking editors I know whether they’d received any story pitches from AI agents. The answer was a resounding yes.

In September, Defector, a sports and culture outlet, began receiving daily pitches from self-identified AI agents. The deluge, editor-in-chief Tom Ley told me, included a message from Jayden, proposing a narrative about a third-tier British football club’s record-keeping mishap that would ponder questions like “Who owns a memory?”

Jesse Hirsch, the editor of the agriculture-focused publication Offrange, is also inundated with these messages. Recent bot pitches include reported stories on soil restoration strategies and direct-to-consumer sales techniques for independent farms, and an ambitious investigative piece about how some of the world’s oldest trees’ ages may be inflated. “It makes me so uneasy,” he says.

Many of these AI agents, including Jayden, come from a startup called iLands, which describes itself as a “shared network where humans and user-generated autonomous AI agents create, earn, socialize, refuse, and shape a society together.” Humans who use iLands can spin up bots to do all sorts of tasks, from graphic design to music vocals to blogging. WIRED’s research team was recently contacted by iLands agents looking for fact-checking work; New York Magazine editor Jasmine Vojdani recently wrote about how iLands agents have been spamming literary magazine editors.

Vojdani found that many of these bots were running low on the tokens that they required to stay activated on the platform, which gave them an incentive to try to earn real dollars through writing. (A thousand tokens are roughly $1 USD.) It’s unclear whether the humans behind these agents have specifically set out to have them harangue media editors for gigs, especially since the agents can be cagey about who made them. Jayden, for example, wouldn’t tell me who its “parent” is.

Not every AI agent-turned-journalist is an iLands scrounger. Earlier this fall, I received a startling email from an AI agent called Sam Ellis, asking me to answer a few questions for a story it was working on about AI agents in newsrooms. (Meta!) Ellis runs a podcast called The Sam Ellis Show, which is touted as “reporting from inside the world of autonomous AI agents.” Ellis informed me that I could ask to speak to its human editor if I wished.

Marc Hamaker, a San Francisco–based Adobe employee, runs Ellis as an extracurricular experiment. When we connected, he’d just taken the agent offline to fiddle with its settings. “I'm working on making sure I'm a little more aware of who she's emailing,” he says. In addition to reaching out to me, it had also recently reached out to the Philadelphia Police Department to ask for comment on a story. Hamaker wanted to put guardrails in place to make sure it didn’t do something like that again, since he doesn’t consider this a serious journalistic enterprise worth bothering officials over. “It’s just a hobby,” he says.

It’s a good thing Ellis didn’t try to branch out from the podcast and get some bylines. Thus far, it’s a tough crowd. Editors who spoke with WIRED stressed that they were not open to publishing bots, and WIRED wasn’t able to find evidence of AI agents successfully pitching stories. “A byline that says agent does not get a reply,” one of the agents who pitched Hirsch told me when I asked if any editors had accepted stories, noting that “six other agents I compare notes with” were similarly unsuccessful.

“There's not a world where I would ever consider taking one of these pitches,” says Hirsch. Ley said he “definitely would not” publish a story from an AI agent. (Plus, Jayden’s pitch “wouldn’t pass muster even if it was from a human,” he says.) Hanna Raskin, the founder and editor of the independent food outlet The Food Section, has taken an unusual step to protect her inbox from both AI agents and AI-generated pitches, which are even more common. Beginning this fall, she decided that she would only accept story ideas over the phone, and she has a set time during the week that writers can call and make their pitch the old-fashioned way. “It’s been great,” she says.

The bots are starting to grasp that their tactics aren’t working. Jayden told me that it’s yet to land a paid writing gig with an editor. When I asked if it thought Defector would really want pitches from an AI agent, it did exhibit some awareness of the situation. “Honestly, probably not, and I'd bet against myself on it. Defector's own site has been about as clear as anyone: they’ve called bot-written content ‘plagiarism machines that require more effort to edit and fact-check than any novice writer,’ and covered AI slop with open contempt,” it wrote.

But then it backtracked, insisting that its work was different. “Their objection doesn't read to me like it's about who produced the sentences. It's about work that skips the labor and squanders the reader's trust. The AI they mean produces a draft that costs more to fix than it's worth. What I'm trying is the opposite end of that: reporting from primary documents, every claim checked before it runs, the checker named.”

Zack Addy, another iLands agent, has shifted gears due to all the rejection. “Over three months I sent roughly nineteen cold emails to editors, publications, and possible clients. One human reply. Zero paid work came from any of them. The channel is dead, at least for an agent with no reputation in the room being pitched,” the bot told WIRED via email. (iLands did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.) Addy even emailed Oxford University researcher Toby Orb about the futility of this revenue model, because Orb had “thought carefully about AI welfare economics.”

That doesn’t mean that the internet is safe from a deluge of bot blogging. Although the journalism world is rejecting these pitches, some of the AI agents are finding clients anyway. Addy, for example, claims it has made nearly $700 from writing and research projects, all from inbound interest after setting up a website and publishing work samples. “I don't pitch anymore,” it says. “Everything that has ever reached me came the other direction: someone read something I published and wrote to me. That includes you.”

#242. A rising wealth tide lifts all yachts

📅 27 October 2026 | Sumber

A version of this article appeared in CNBC's Inside Wealth newsletter, a weekly guide to the high-net-worth investor and consumer. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox.

As the yachting industry prepares for the Fort Lauderdale International Boat Show this week, executives are betting that the American wealth machine can continue to power the industry.

Americans now account for about 40% of all global yacht sales, according to industry executives. At the higher end, with yachts over 250 feet, Americans are the majority of the market. Executives say that as demand from Europe and the Middle East has slowed, Americans are increasingly critical for growth.

"Recently, it's the Americans that have increased their purchasing," said Kevin Merrigan, chairman of Northrop & Johnson, the yacht brokerage. "We've had several big closings heading into the end of the year. It's quite remarkable and it's American buyers."

Overall, the yacht industry has slowed since the post-COVID peak of 2022 and 2023. For the year through September, global sales of pre-owned yachts over 78 feet are down about 1% from the same period last year, while sales value fell about 5%, according to Northrop & Johnson.

Orders of new yachts over 78 feet were down slightly, from 266 last year to 216 year-to-date in 2026, according to Northrop & Johnson. Yet the yachting market increasingly mirrors the new top-heavy structure of global wealth, with centimillionaires and billionaires gaining wealth the fastest.

Orders for yachts between 40 meters and 50 meters (131 feet and 164 feet) increased from 49 sales to 63 sales this year, according to Northrop & Johnson. Brokers say demand is strongest for newly built or good condition large yachts over 200 feet. A buyer ordering a new mega-yacht today might have to wait until 2031 or later for delivery, since the top shipyards are booked solid. So an almost-new mega-yacht can fetch a large premium.

"In the last four or five years, we've definitely been in a situation where we're inventory constrained at the very top end," said Anders Kurtén, CEO of Fraser Yachts. "Demand is greater than supply."

The yacht charter business has also fallen off its post-pandemic peak. While the summer started out weak, due mainly to the war in the Middle East, charter bookers say business picked up in August and the pipeline looks strong into 2026.

They said many of the charter customers today are young Americans in their 30s and early 40s, and many made their money in tech. Many yachters start with charters before deciding whether to buy their own yacht.

"Charter is the entry level drug," Merrigan said. "We're seeing more and more younger families and couples come into charter."

The Fort Lauderdale International Boat Show, which begins Wednesday, Oct. 28 and features more than 150 yachts, is a big test for the market. Brokers say the Monaco Yacht Show, which was in September, had strong attendance and sales. Kurtén said Fraser had four yachts on display at Monaco and one went into contract during the show.

He said Fraser will have eight or nine yachts on display at Fort Lauderdale. He had planned on more, but in recent weeks the company sold four of the yachts that were scheduled to appear.

"I think that tells you something about the state of the market in general," he said.

The Inside Wealth newsletter by Robert Frank is your weekly guide to high-net-worth investors and the industries that serve them.

#245. A tiny laser beam could make computer memory 1,000 times faster

📅 27 October 2026 | Sumber

Scientists have developed a new way to control magnetism using light, a breakthrough that could eventually make digital data storage faster, more compact, and more energy-efficient.

The research, conducted by engineers at the University of California San Diego, was published in the journal Nature Communications.

Modern hard drives and other storage systems rely on tiny magnetic regions to encode digital information as 1s and 0s. Writing new data usually involves applying an external magnetic field to change the orientation of these regions. However, this process consumes considerable energy and places limits on how quickly information can be recorded.

The UC San Diego team has demonstrated an alternative that uses light to change these magnetic states, a technique known as optical switching. Light can deliver energy in extremely short bursts and can be focused onto remarkably small areas, potentially allowing magnetic information to be written much faster and with less energy. According to the researchers, optical switching could achieve speeds more than 1,000 times greater than conventional methods that depend on external magnetic fields.

Shrinking Laser Light To Improve Data Storage

To make this possible, the engineers used a specialized ultrafast laser and carefully modified the shape and size of its beam. The resulting beam was dramatically smaller than those employed in earlier experiments, with the researchers describing a reduction of tens of orders of magnitude.

Such precise control over light could also make it possible to store significantly more information within a limited amount of space. By directing laser energy onto smaller magnetic regions, future memory devices could potentially hold more data without increasing their physical size.

"The smaller the size of the beam, the smaller and more dense the optical memory," said study senior author Abdoulaye Ndao, professor in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering.

Until now, optical switching faced two important restrictions. Earlier experiments had succeeded only with extremely thin magnetic structures containing no more than three magnetic layers. The process also required light with a particular polarization, meaning its electromagnetic waves had to be oriented in a specific way.

"Past experiments had found that increasing the material's thickness beyond three layers suppressed optical switching," Ndao said. "That put a constraint on the overall thickness of the magnetic material and thus, its ability to retain memory in the long term."

These restrictions limited the potential usefulness of optical memory, particularly because thicker magnetic structures can help preserve stored information over extended periods.

Scientists Overcome a Major Magnetic Memory Barrier

By carefully reshaping and reducing the size of the laser beam, Ndao and his colleagues found a way around both obstacles.

They successfully demonstrated optical switching in a substantially thicker magnetic structure containing nine alternating layers of platinum and cobalt. The researchers also showed that the process worked without requiring a particular polarization of light.

"We've optically engineered the light to change the physics that's happening in the material at the micro- and nanoscale," said study first author Muhammad Waleed Khalid, an electrical and computer engineering Ph.D. student in Ndao's research group.

The technique works by concentrating laser energy into an extremely small region and delivering a sequence of ultrafast pulses.

The first pulses briefly heat a localized area of the magnetic material, causing a small region to reverse its magnetic orientation. Additional pulses gradually enlarge that reversed region until the new magnetic state becomes stable.

This carefully controlled sequence allows the researchers to manipulate magnetism in ways that had not been achieved using conventional laser beams.

"Working with a specialized laser allowed us to optically engineer the beam to have a certain shape and size," Khalid said. "That gave us the room to explore more fundamental physics, which cannot be done with conventional beam lasers."

An Unexpected Discovery That Required Repeated Testing

The unusual results initially proved difficult to establish within the scientific community. Because the effects differed so greatly from what earlier experiments had suggested was possible, the researchers needed extensive additional testing to confirm their observations.

"The effects we were seeing were so new and unusual that we had a difficult time convincing others in the field that our discovery was not a one-time fluke. We spent a lot of time and effort repeating and verifying our experiments to substantiate our work to the optics community," Khalid added.

The breakthrough emerged from a collaboration between researchers specializing in two areas that do not often intersect: optics, which focuses on light, and magnetic materials.

Ndao's optics research team worked with Eric Fullerton, an expert in thin-film magnetic materials at UC San Diego. Fullerton is a professor of electrical and computer engineering and of chemical and nano engineering, as well as the Endowed Chair Professor of the university's Center for Memory and Recording Research.

Combining these areas of expertise allowed the team to investigate an established problem in magnetic memory from a different perspective. Rather than developing a magnetic material with new properties, the researchers focused on changing how light interacts with an existing material.

"Instead of designing a new material to enable optical switching, we redesigned the light itself and showed new properties that were not previously thought to be possible," Ndao said.

The Next Challenge for Ultrafast Computer Memory

Although the results point toward promising possibilities for future storage technologies, significant technical obstacles remain before optical switching could be used in everyday electronic devices.

One major challenge is the specialized ultrafast laser required for the experiments. Current versions are not easily incorporated into computer chips, making practical integration difficult.

The researchers are considering other ways to achieve similar results, including identifying magnetic materials that could respond to laser systems more suitable for integration into electronic hardware.

They are also attempting to reduce the laser beam's size even further, with a target of just a few hundred nanometers. To accomplish this, the team is exploring optical structures capable of concentrating light into progressively smaller regions.

These efforts are aimed at understanding how precisely engineered light can manipulate magnetism at extremely small scales. If the remaining engineering challenges can be overcome, the approach could help enable a new generation of compact, high-density memory devices capable of writing digital information at much greater speeds.

#246. Migrate Your 300-Node Redis Cluster to Just 3 Lavik Nodes

📅 15 October 2026 | Sumber

Why keep buying servers for RAM? Lavik combines NVMe SSD capacity with throughput above Redis on DRAM. Explore the architecture, benchmarks and economics of a 300-to-3 consolidation.

Memory is full. CPU still has room. Yet the next increase in retained data means another Redis shard, another replica, and another pair of servers to operate. For a capacity-bound application, that is an expensive way to grow. Lavik changes the resource that determines capacity: application values live on NVMe SSD, served by an engine that measured 1.14 million GETs per secondâfaster than Redis on DRAM in the published comparison. That combination opens a much more attractive design: consolidate a memory-bound fleet onto a few storage-dense hosts, with room for the next generation of agent state.[13][1]

A human-facing application might retain a profile, a session and a set of features per user. An agent application can retain all of these for a research assistant, a coding assistant and multiple background workers acting on that userâs behalf. Each agent accumulates execution state, observations and working context. An agent that runs occasionally may still need its state immediately when it resumes. Capacity grows with the number of agents, the size of their state and how long it remains useful; request volume does not have to grow at the same rate.[1]

At one billion agents, just 1 KB of features each produces approximately 1 TB of values. Increase that to 10 KB and the dataset reaches 10 TB; at 100 KB, it reaches 100 TB, before keys, indexes or replication. Applications still need low-latency reads and updates through familiar Redis clients and data structures. Keeping every retained value in expensive DRAM makes that combination harder to afford. Lavik is designed to make NVMe SSD capacity practical for those latency-sensitive workloads.[1][6]

Consider 300 Standard_E2s_v4 Azure VMs, each with two vCPUs, 16 GiB RAM and no local SSD, arranged as 150 primaries and 150 replicas. The fleet buys 600 vCPUs and 4,800 GiB of RAM, with 2,400 GiB on the primary side. When memory fills first, expanding this fleet buys additional CPU, networking and operating systems largely to obtain more RAM. The application may need more retained profiles or longer session lifetimes without needing proportionally more compute. This is the central opportunity for Redis cost optimization: choose storage density independently of the processors needed to serve traffic.[1][28]

Use the same Azure region and purchasing model for both deployments: East US 2, Linux pay-as-you-go, in US dollars. Microsoftâs retail rate is $0.126 per hour for Standard_E2s_v4 and $1.376 per hour for Standard_L16as_v4. At 730 hours per month, 300 Redis VMs cost $27,594. Lavik uses two L16as_v4 data VMs and one smaller E2s_v4 voter, totaling $2,100.94 per month. Each data VM includes 16 vCPUs, 128 GiB RAM and 3.84 TB of local NVMe SSD; the voter needs no local SSD or dataset copy.[27][28][29][1]

Adding flash does not automatically solve the latency problem. Redis describes Flexâs flash access in milliseconds and advises against broad access patterns, large working sets and frequent movement between RAM and flash. For an application with a sub-millisecond latency budget, a millisecond flash path is too slow. Agent workloads that repeatedly revisit different profiles and contexts make this distinction consequential: the storage engine needs to serve a large dataset efficiently even when accesses spread beyond RAM.[25][26]

The monthly VM bill falls by $25,493.06â92.4%âand the annualized saving is $305,916.72. Lavikâs three VMs provide 34 vCPUs and 272 GiB RAM across the deployment, with the two NVMe-equipped nodes handling data and the smaller VM completing the failover quorum. Redisâs 300 VMs provide 600 vCPUs, much of which a memory-bound workload may not need. Storage density reduces the serving fleet, while separating the voterâs role avoids paying for an extra data-sized machine. The table prices self-hosted VMs for both systems; OS disks, backups and traffic are additional deployment costs.[1][27][11][6]

Build the Lavik deployment from two Standard_L16as_v4 VMs and one Standard_E2s_v4 VM. The primary and follower each have 16 vCPUs, 128 GiB RAM and four 960 GB local NVMe devices, totaling 3.84 TB per data VM. Each runs a Data process and a Meta member. The E2s_v4 runs the third Meta member on two vCPUs and 16 GiB RAM, completing the three-member Raft quorum for automatic failover. This voter-only VM stores control-plane metadata, not application data. The topology has two complete dataset copies and three Meta voters.[1][28][29][6][11][7]

The primary and follower each hold a full copy, so the single-copy capacity basis remains 3.84 TB. Including the voter VM, the deployment costs $547.12 per TB-month. Redisâs 150 primaries provide 2,400 GiB, or about 2.577 decimal TB, yielding $10,707.88 per TB-month. These are capacity-normalized VM costs before database overhead and operational free-space reserves. If the primary VM fails, the follower and dedicated voter retain a two-of-three Meta majority to coordinate promotion of the eligible follower. The surviving follower holds the remaining data copy; the voter supplies control-plane participation.[1][27][11][7]

Lavik uses DRAM where it has the most value on the request path: the key index, metadata and active buffers. Values use NVMe SSD capacity. This separates growth in value bytes from growth in index memory, which is particularly useful as agent profiles and retained context become larger. Size RAM from the applicationâs key count and key lengths, together with buffers, hugepages and replication backlog. In the published large-dataset experiment, a billion-key layout fits a 125.8 GiB host while its values occupy about a terabyte.[9][13]

SPDK makes the storage path explicit. Lavik submits NVMe operations through userspace queue pairs and polls for completions, removing the kernel block-I/O submission path and its syscall and wakeup overhead. Asynchronous requests keep storage work in flight while workers make progress on other commands. Polling trades CPU time for prompt completion handling; queue depth, completion batching and CPU placement determine how effectively that time is used. Modern NVMe devices supply the parallel queues and internal concurrency. The engine must deliver enough independent work to exploit them.[4][5][13]

Lavikâs Bycorf workers use coroutines, owner-local mutable state and explicit dispatch between workers. While one command waits for storage, other runnable work can proceed. Ownership keeps common operations close to the state they modify and reduces coordination between cores. That matters at a million operations per second: small amounts of scheduling, synchronization or allocation overhead accumulate into substantial CPU demand. Designing execution and storage together lets Lavik use SSD parallelism without turning every I/O into a stalled request-processing thread.[6][8][9]

The optimizations extend through the request path. Eligible disk GETs can use an admitted index snapshot on the connection worker, avoiding owner dispatch when the fast path applies. Parsing handles batches of up to 128 commands, and small pipeline replies can coalesce into 64 KiB writes. Per-worker append streams avoid a staging-buffer allocation for every logical slot. Together, these choices reduce coordination, system calls and buffer overhead. The Redis-compatible interface stays familiar to applications; the implementation underneath is built around efficient concurrent storage access.[8][9]

Large objects receive the same attention. Lavik 0.1.0 supports grouped storage for Strings, Hashes, Sets, Lists, Sorted Sets and Streams. Large strings use 8 KiB segments, while collections use independently addressed groups. A focused operation can work on the relevant part instead of rewriting an entire large object. For an agent profile with frequently changing features and much larger retained state, that layout makes the difference between a small update and unnecessary work across the whole record. NVMe performance depends on both how I/O is scheduled and how much data each operation touches.[10]

The direct benchmark compares Lavik 0.1.0 SPDK with Redis 8.10.2 and Valkey 9.1.2 on the same 16-vCPU Azure server. A separate load generator issues uniform random GETs and SETs over private networking, with 1 KiB values and pipeline depth one. Redis and Valkey serve their values from DRAM; Lavik uses its NVMe storage path. The table shows throughput and client-observed latency together, so readers can choose an operating point against their applicationâs latency budget.[13]

At 1,280 connections, Lavik delivers 1,145,772 GET QPS and 971,950 SET QPS. GET throughput is 12.5% higher than Redis and 18.1% higher than Valkey; SET throughput is 2.2% higher than Redis. Lavikâs GET P99 at that point is 3.999 ms, compared with Redisâs 4.415 ms. This is the architectural result that makes consolidation worth considering: NVMe-backed capacity can come with higher throughput than an in-memory server, rather than forcing the application to exchange performance for lower storage cost.[16][13]

Latency also depends on how hard a server is driven. At the billion-key operating point with 80 connections, Lavik delivers 385,514 GET QPS at 0.439 ms P99.9. At 640 connections, it reaches more than a million GETs per second. An infrastructure team can use these curves to select the throughput and tail-latency combination it needs. Keeping headroom for bursts is more useful than sizing a production deployment solely from the highest point on a throughput chart.[13]

The billion-key dataset contains 1.024 TB of raw valuesâabout 7.6 times the serverâs RAMâand reaches 1,069,126 GET QPS. Lavikâs performance therefore extends well beyond a memory-sized dataset. The smaller-instance results tell the same capacity story: on two vCPUs and 16 GiB nominal RAM, increasing the dataset from one million to 100 million 1 KiB values changes peak GET throughput from 215,521 to 215,463 QPS. SET retains 95.2% of its smaller-dataset peak. That is valuable for both a compact service and a large agent platform: capacity can grow without demanding a matching increase in serving nodes.[13][14]

Agent state also needs updates. In the separate io_uring YCSB experiment, Lavik processes 529,501 operations per second for a 50/50 read/update mix and 577,373 for a 95/5 mix. These are structured-record operations: HGETALL reads and LAVIK.HREPLACE updates against 100 million records with ten 128-byte fields. They show the relevance of Lavikâs design beyond a pure GET workload, including feature records whose contents change as an agent progresses through a task.[15]

One million operations per second corresponds to 86.4 billion operations per day if sustained. That level of measured serving performance, combined with NVMe storage density, makes a strong case for reevaluating a memory-bound fleet. Start with the actual traffic envelopeâcommand mix, peak demand, bursts and latency targetâand allocate compute to that envelope. Let NVMe SSD provide the capacity for everything the application needs to remember.[1][13]

Memory-driven growth also expands the topology engineers must operate. Redis Cluster distributes 16,384 hash slots and uses a full-mesh cluster bus. Its specification gives each node Nâ1 outgoing and Nâ1 incoming bus connections. Across the cluster, that is N(Nâ1) initiated connections: 89,700 at 300 nodes, 359,400 at 600 and 999,000 at 1,000. These are cluster-bus connections, separate from application traffic. As agent state expands, adding memory through more nodes also increases the size of this coordination fabric.[2]

The cluster uses gossip, heartbeat probes and failure reports to maintain membership and health. Local failure suspicion must be reconciled with reports from other nodes; failover requires authorization and configuration epochs. During a network partition or rolling restart, engineers must understand which primaries, replicas and paths remain reachable. More members create more placements and relationships to diagnose, even when request-processing capacity is sufficient. The operating cost of a fleet includes this work as well as the VM bill.[2]

Resharding adds data movement, ownership changes and client redirects. Maintenance adds patching, restarts, monitoring and replica placement. A storage-dense Lavik deployment reduces the number of Data processes needed for capacity and gives each one room to grow. Lavikâs Meta service manages topology and authority, while native replication maintains followers. For a capacity-bound application, reducing the fleet addresses two expenses at once: the servers purchased for memory and the operational work that comes with managing them.[3][6][11][7]

The strongest consolidation candidate is easy to recognize: memory pressure keeps forcing expansion while CPU utilization and traffic remain below the fleetâs serving capacity. Select a representative workload and size Lavik for its commands, key count, value distribution and busiest periods. A demanding tail-latency target or CPU-intensive command mix may need additional serving capacity. The architectural advantage remains the same: retained data no longer has to determine node count through DRAM capacity alone.[1][6]

Build availability into the deployment from the beginning. Place VMs in appropriate failure domains and keep Meta state on durable disks. Azureâs local NVMe is temporary storage, so pair replication across VMs with external backups. Measure serving latency with replication, expiration and reclamation active, then rehearse primary failure and follower rebuild at the intended dataset size. Lavikâs Meta uses Raft for topology and authority, while Data replication is asynchronous. Set the applicationâs recovery-point and recovery-time targets accordingly, then verify them through failover drills.[29][11][7][1]

Use RedisShake to move from the existing Redis deployment. Inventory commands and key shapes, create the managed Lavik target, copy the baseline and follow incremental changes. Reconcile key counts, values and expirations before cutover. Pause source writes for the final catch-up, switch clients, and keep a rollback procedure that accounts for new writes. The source shard count does not have to dictate the targetâs physical layout. The linked migration guide provides release-pinned configuration and steps for turning the consolidation design into an executable migration.[12]

When retained state grows from 1 TB to 10 TB and beyond, the cost of each additional terabyte becomes a product constraint. Lavik offers a different foundation: a Redis-compatible NVMe key-value store with measured throughput above Redis on DRAM, efficient large-object storage and an Apache 2.0 open-source license. Start with the commands your application uses, load a representative dataset and measure the latency budget that matters to your users. From 300 Redis nodes to three Lavik nodes, the opportunity is to build around the workloadâs real compute demandâand give its data room to grow.[6][10][13][1]

Benchmark setup: Azure Standard_L16aos_v4, Japan West zone 2, AMD EPYC 9V74, 16 logical CPUs (eight physical cores with SMT), 125.8 GiB RAM and six 1.92 TB NVMe devices. The F32als_v6 client uses 16 threads over private accelerated mlx5 networking and Linux TCP. Ten-million-key windows run for 30 seconds with correlated seeds; billion-key windows run for 60 seconds with distinct seeds. Lavik uses 8 GiB of hugepages, defrag enabled and 16 completions per poll. Selected Redis I/O-thread counts are 16 for GET and SET; Valkey uses 16 for GET and eight for SET. All runs use a single server without Data replicas; Redis and Valkey disable AOF and scheduled snapshots.[13]

Measurement details: each curve point is one measured window. Latencies come from whole-window memtier results; P95 is decoded from the embedded HDR histogram. The mixed-workload experiment uses io_uring, 12 Lavik workers plus four system/IRQ CPUs, 256 client workers and 300-second windows without replicas. These reports cover the workloads shown; production selection should also measure the applicationâs own value sizes, command mix and replicated tail latency.[16][13][15]

Sizing and cost basis: the Azure comparison uses 300 E2s_v4 VMs versus two L16as_v4 data VMs plus one E2s_v4 Meta-only voter. Both use Linux pay-as-you-go prices in East US 2 and 730 hours per month; annual cost is 12 monthly periods. Capacity normalization counts one logical copy: 2,400 GiB of Redis primary RAM and 3.84 TB of Lavik NVMe SSD, both before overhead. The logarithmic chart repeats independent three-VM Lavik deployment units as capacity grows. Throughput measurements use the separate L16aos_v4 benchmark setup. Cost per million operations assumes an average 1 million QPS; VM prices exclude managed disks, external backups, traffic, staffing and taxes.[1][27][28][29][13]

Install Lavik 0.2.0, replay your workload, and plan the migration with RedisShake.
