#289. What Marco Rubio’s sidestepping of New Delhi says about the US’s stance on India

📅 27 October 2026 | Sumber

Rubio’s decision not to meet Narendra Modi last week was seen by some as a snub – but by focusing on business leaders and oil, the secretary of state made American priorities clear. Plus: the artist bringing a female perspective to men’s clothing

Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

When the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, visited India for the second time this year, headlines concentrated on who he met and where he went.

The fact that Rubio bypassed New Delhi and did not meet the prime minister, Narendra Modi, during his trip last week, and instead traveled to the financial capital, Mumbai, where he met India’s foreign minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar (pictured top with Rubio), and business leaders, did not go unnoticed. Nor did his decision to travel to Jamnagar, the small Gujarati town that is home to Reliance Industries’ colossal oil refinery complex.

Bilateral ties between the two countries have come under strain under the second Trump administration, particularly over tariffs and India’s purchase of Russian oil. Yet, Rubio’s return to India just five months after his first visit as secretary of state signals that the country remains useful for president Donald Trump’s ambitions after all.

As director of the South Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Milan Vaishnav has spent a decade tracking India’s place in the world, particularly its ties with the US. Vaishnav has described Trump 2.0 as “unbound” marking a new era in India-US relations.

Tracking foreign affairs, he told me, is a minefield right now. From the White House’s transactional approach to global alliances, ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and consequential elections around the world, politics is changing at a pace that means all predictions are off the table. “I think anyone who tells you they know exactly what is going on and how it fits into their neat theory of the world is lying to you,” says Vaishnav.

I asked him about the many confusing aspects of the US-India relationship, from the hostile political rhetoric to the US embrace of Pakistan, as well as Rubio’s latest visit.

Ahead of Rubio’s visit, several commentators noted the secretary of state’s “unusual” itinerary. Vaishnav thought the pre-visit chatter about Rubio skipping Delhi to visit Mumbai and Jamnagar was overblown. “Not every bilateral meeting has to take place in a national capital,” he says.

But that doesn’t mean it wasn’t noteworthy. “I do think the choice of venues was intentional. This administration and, particularly, this president, sees foreign policy through the lens of ‘deal-making’. And if you’re trying to drum up business deals, what better place to visit than Mumbai?” he says.

The Jamnagar visit, where Rubio met Mukesh Ambani, the chair of Reliance, also indicates some politicking. “At a time when petrol prices are extremely high in the United States and are likely to be a major issue in the 3 November midterm elections, the administration wants to show that it is doing everything it can to bring them down. India is a major consumer of oil, but it is also a major exporter of refined petroleum products,” says Vaishnav. “One of Rubio’s objectives was to encourage Reliance and, by extension, India to process more Venezuelan crude [oil],” he added.

While this could present an opportunity for India to advance relations, it’s not a given: the US president remains, after all – and to put it lightly – mercurial.

“The biggest plot twist for me has been the Trump administration’s embrace of Pakistan after the May 2025 conflict with India,” says Vaishnav. Pakistan’s standing in Washington had eroded over the years, especially under Joe Biden, who left office without ever having made a presidential phone call to his counterpart in Pakistan. “Many officials in Congress had grown exhausted with Pakistan’s double game, speaking the language of partnership on the one hand while undermining US interests on the other,” says Vaishnav.

But, after coming to power the second time, Trump thanked the country for its help in nabbing a suspect linked to a 2021 bombing in Afghanistan that killed 13 US service members. This reversal in Pakistan’s fortunes gathered pace after the May conflict with India, which Trump took credit for ending. In June, he welcomed Asim Munir, Pakistan’s army chief, to the White House, after Munir called for the president to be nominated for the Nobel peace prize.

“I chalk up the reversal to a few factors: Trump’s well-known strongman envy, Pakistan’s savvy diplomacy, and the prospect of energy and crypto deals involving members of Trump’s inner circle,” says Vaishnav. For him, it isyet another demonstration of how much weight Trump places on deals, transactions and short-term wins. “For New Delhi, this means Modi’s personal rapport with Trump and 25 years of investment in the bilateral relationship offer no guarantee against a 180-degree reversal in US policy,” he adds.

In a recent piece, Vaishnav’s colleague Sameer Lalwani pointed out that the US relationship with India remains more resilient than the political rhetoric may suggest with quiet, but nonetheless strategic, progress being made.

As Lalwani points out, bilateral trade reached a record high between India and the US in 2025; nearly $68bn worth of AI infrastructure investment in India has been pledged by US technology companies; and the two countries have carried out record number of joint military exercises this year.

Despite these wins, in terms of future bilateral relations, “there are at least three reasons for caution,” warns Vaishnav. First, he points to the onslaught of US actions that have dented Indian interests. Trump had imposed a punitive 50% tariff on India in 2025, which was reduced to 18% earlier this year, but without a comprehensive trade deal being reached. Second, on immigration, the White House’s H-1B visa and green card restrictions have disproportionately affected Indian workers in Silicon Valley.

“This has created a real trust deficit on the Indian side, and with good reason,” says Vaishnav. The frustration was on display earlier this month, when New Delhi branded remarks made by the US vice-president, JD Vance, about Indian professionals as “deeply offensive”. Furthermore, Vaishnav argues that while governments and private sector firms might be great at making announcements, they’re not always a guarantee of delivery.

His final caution is how political tensions can have a chilling effect. The trade negotiations offer a telling example: in January, the US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, blamed the lack of a trade deal on Modi’s failure to phone Trump, a characterisation that New Delhi has disputed. Vaishnav says: “Much of the progress we are seeing is the product of decisions made years ago. It is one thing to keep existing projects moving, but turbulence in the relationship could make new initiatives a heavier lift.”

If India is serious about making its ambition to be a global powerhouse a reality, Vaishnav thinks there’s a clearcut way to win. “I would argue that the most important investment is political – ensuring India remains a robust, inclusive, participatory democracy,” he says. “On the economic front, India has made massive new investments in physical and digital infrastructure. But the returns on those investments will be limited unless the government doubles down on reforms: more efficient dispute resolution, an impartial legal system, even-handed tax enforcementand regulatory certainty.”

Ultimately, neither side can afford to treat the other as expendable. The test now is whether strategic foundations can hold at a time of global political upheaval.

Student protests | Bikaner House, one of Delhi’s premier arts venues, asked visual artist Raihan Vadra to remove from his show more than 70 photographs that featured recent student protests. Vadra, the son of the Congress leader, Priyanka Gandhi, defended his work and also refused a request to remove images featuring the national flag. In a press statement, the venue said certain photos were “inconsistent” with its policy.

Niha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern India

Fashion | Designer Sabyasachi Mukherjee, celebrated for his maximalist aesthetic, hosted a Diwali party at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art. In September, he unveiled a high-jewellery collection inspired by the Byzantine, in collaboration with the museum.

Air pollution | Emergency measures, including a ban on coal-fired tandoors in restaurants and restrictions on diesel generators, have come into effect in Delhi, as air quality dropped to the poor category at the onset of the annual pollution season.

A recommendation from someone with great taste

Film-maker Ritu Sarin, director of the annual Dharamshala international film festival, which runs from 29 October to 1 November, suggests a film from this year’s lineup:

“Shot over three years on real locations, Anmol Sidhu’s sophomore feature, Flowers of Acacia, follows wedding orchestra dancers in rural Punjab with a gaze that allows all the large brutalities and smaller intimacies to shine through. Sidhu’s confident, consummate grasp of the medium is on full display in terrifying scenes that stretch to the edge of what is palatable. The camera refuses to look away.”

That’s the number of trees Mumbai’s municipal authorities authorised to be felled over five months this year, to make way for development works, according to the Indian Express. Of these, about 3,500 will be permanently removed, while the rest will be replanted elsewhere.

Prarthna Singh has consistently placed the female identity at the heart of her artistic practice, documenting Indian women’s aspirations and acts of rebellion in male-dominated spaces. When commissioned to photograph rkivecity’s menswear line, made from discarded clothes reworked into new garments, she turned that same gaze outward. The setting was the acclaimed 151-year-old Mayo College boys’ school in Ajmer, Rajasthan – Singh attended the linked girls’ school, and credits it with shaping her rebellious spirit.

“I was thinking about how I could bring a sense of intimacy and camaraderie of boarding-school life to the images, because that exists,” she told me. One image shows a pair of hands holding another boy’s jacket, the faces left out of the frame, so the garment stands in for the familiarity they share. Seeing this work against the backdrop of students taking to the streets to fight for their rights lends the series a lasting significance. “This was just my way of showing all of this is connected. These worlds are not existing separately,” said Singh.

#294. Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi ‘sounds strong’ but is isolated, son says

📅 25 October 2026 | Sumber

Kim Aris tells the Guardian chance to speak with detained Nobel laureate was ‘public relations’ move from military leaders

Myanmar’s former democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi appears to be in good physical and mental health but is living in near-complete isolation, her son has said after the first call with his 81-year-old mother in more than five years.

“She still sounds certainly all there mentally, and physically she sounds strong,” Kim Aris said. “I don’t think she has anybody outside of the military or the police around her, so essentially she’s been held in solitary confinement from what I gather.”

After being deposed in a 2021 military coup, the Nobel Peace prize laureate has been moved to an unspecified location in the capital. “I’m still not entirely sure where she is,” said Aris. “I think it’s a residence in Naypyidaw, which is fenced off and it has a scrubby bit of land around it.”

Aris, who has lived in the UK most of his life and whose late father was a British historian, was allowed to speak to his mother on Thursday at the Myanmar embassy in London. While he welcomed the chance to talk, he said the invitation was part of a “public relations” campaign by the country’s military leaders.

The former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing has sought to rebuild international diplomatic ties, and in April switched his military fatigues for civilian clothes after elections that were widely condemned as a sham.

Activists have long demanded “proof of life” for Aung San Suu Kyi, as well as scores of other political prisoners. In August, she was finally photographed during a Red Cross visit. Last week, a government spokesperson published images of her smiling in a wood-panelled room as officials delivered two gardening books given to her as gifts by Britain’s King Charles. A paper calendar on the wall behind her showed the date.

Aris said these photo-ops were well-known stunts that the regime had used before to pretend his mother, a national icon, was being treated fairly. The daughter of the assassinated national independence hero Gen Aung San has spent much of her life since the late 1980s in and out of house arrest for leading pro-democracy movements.

“She remains completely shut off from the rest of the world. I think she’s unaware of what’s happening outside of where she is because she’s not allowed any newspapers or radio or television,” Aris said. “She’s been locked up for five years on trumped-up, politically motivated charges and she should be free.”

Ruled for decades by generals and suffering from western sanctions, Myanmar experienced a brief democratic moment after Aung San Suu Kyi was allowed to run in a 2015 election that her party overwhelmingly won. She took up the role of “state counsellor” under a civilian-military power-sharing agreement.

Her international reputation was soon tarnished after the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims. Aung San Suu Kyi flew to the international court of justice in The Hague, where she said she acknowledged military units might have used “disproportionate force”, but defended the government against accusations of genocide.

Aris said that his mother was never “silent” on the Rohingya crisis and what she said on the issue “could fill volumes”. Under her leadership, Myanmar launched a domestic inquiry and appointed the former UN chief Kofi Annan to head a commission.

He added that as state counsellor, Aung San Suu Kyi was “always walking on a tightrope”, knowing the military could strip her of her fragile power at any moment.

“The very hard-won nascent democracy that she was trying to lead was holding on to things by a thread,” he said. “The military could have taken over at any point, and they were doing their best to make my mother’s situation a lot more difficult and to undermine her position. And I think in that respect they did a pretty good job.”

The 2021 power grab by the military triggered a civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to conflict monitors.

Aris said the level of public global support for his mother had “dwindled incredibly” since the Rohingya crisis and that the whole country was now suffering from a lack of international attention. While many governments have called for Aung San Suu Kyi’s release, she is not treated as the beloved international figure that she once was.

“Never mind my mother, the fact that people ignore what’s happening in Burma shouldn’t be down to what was being done to the Rohingya,” he said, using the country’s former name. “And that seems to be the case sometimes, that people say: ‘Oh, well, look how the Rohingya were treated. We can ignore what’s happening in Burma.’”

#295. Israel election puts Netanyahu’s wartime leadership on the line as Trump urges voters to return him to power

📅 26 October 2026 | Sumber

Israeli voters will head to the polls Tuesday in an election with implications beyond the country’s borders.

It is Israel’s first election since Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, which killed around 1,200 people and saw more than 250 abducted. The Palestinian Ministry of Health says Israel’s subsequent military campaign in Gaza has killed more than 74,500 people. It is also the first vote since the U.S. and Israel began their joint war against Iran in February.

With defense at the forefront of the debate for all the main contenders, tens of thousands of Israeli citizens are believed to have flown home to cast their votes in what is expected to be a tight-knit race.

Israelis vote for parties rather than directly electing a prime minister, with the Knesset’s 120 seats allocated through proportional representation. Parties must win at least 3.25% of the national vote to enter parliament.

Because outright majorities are rare, parties typically form coalitions. The president asks a Knesset member — usually the leader best placed to assemble a 61-seat majority — to form a government. If repeated attempts fail, another election can be called.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who leads the right-wing Likud party, returned to power in late 2022 with a coalition including far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties. The alliance has since been strained by disputes over a Gaza ceasefire and the conscription of ultra-Orthodox men.

Recent polls put both Netanyahu's bloc and the main opposition bloc, led by centrist former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, short of the 61 seats needed to govern, making smaller parties potentially decisive.

Arab parties are also in the running, but most of the main Jewish parties have ruled out alliances with them. More than 20% of Israel's population is Arab, but Arab parties have rarely joined governing coalitions.

The impending vote is effectively a referendum on Netanyahu, with the Hamas attacks having "transformed Israeli society," according to László Csicsmann, a Middle East expert at Corvinus University of Budapest in Hungary.

"Israel has been at war since October 7, 2023, and the so-called 'seven-front war' launched by Netanyahu has undoubtedly worn down Israeli society," he told CNBC. "The side that can better convince voters that it can protect the population is likely to win. Other campaign issues include mandatory military service, which is particularly sensitive for religious Jewish parties and Haredi communities."

Military service is compulsory for most Jewish, Druze and Circassian Israelis over 18, while most other Arab Israelis are exempt. The conscription of ultra-Orthodox men remains a major legal and political dispute.

The economic toll of the war is also a major issue, Csicsmann said.

"Due to the war and high military spending, economic issues are also dominating the political campaign," he told CNBC, noting that Israel currently spends around 8% of its gross domestic product on military expenditure. "In addition, nearly every family has a soldier or reservist who has been called up and has left their job for months."

Defense and security are also at the forefront of the election, said Daniel Schatz, a political scientist and former visiting scholar at Harvard, Stanford and Georgetown.

"For Israel, the stakes include restoring confidence in government and deciding how military power translates into lasting security," he told CNBC in an email. "For its neighbors and international partners, the question is whether the next government can turn battlefield achievements into workable political arrangements."

Schatz said that while Netanyahu's supporters see the incumbent prime minister as "an experienced leader confronting formidable threats," his critics see failures of preparedness, accountability and strategic direction.

In September, book extracts published by Israeli newspaper Haaretz alleged that Netanyahu had been warned that Hamas was planning a major offensive around a week before the Oct. 7 attacks. Netanyahu called those claims an "absolute lie," and has reportedly filed a defamation lawsuit against the newspaper.

But Schatz told CNBC that any lingering dissatisfaction with Netanyahu should not be confused with support for the left.

"Some voters want different leadership precisely because they believe it would deliver security more effectively," he said.

He added that a change in prime minister and the governing coalition would also be unlikely to produce a dramatic shift in Israel's stance on Palestinian statehood, Iran and other foreign policy issues.

Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party is running on a manifesto promising "security without compromise," along with pledges to maintain a free economy and financial markets and a bid to strengthen "Israel as a regional and technological power."

Eisenkot's Yashar party says it wants to make Israel a "democratic, powerful, progressive and secure" country, and it also has a focus on national security – including a proposed policy of integrating ultra-Orthodox and Arab communities into compulsory military service.

Farzan Sabet, senior analyst at the Eurasia Group think tank, told CNBC the main blocs competing for power are "quite hawkish on security" and would have comparable policies across key areas like confronting Iran and Hezbollah in Lebanon.

But he added that a new coalition government composed mainly of anti-Netanyahu bloc parties would "probably prefer to review the Israeli strategy towards Tehran" before pursuing any major escalation.

The U.S. and Israel have reportedly drawn up plans for possible renewed strikes on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3, while Iran's army chief has said it is ready for "asymmetric warfare."

The outcome could be consequential for U.S.-Israel relations.

Trump reiterated his endorsement of Netanyahu in a Truth Social post on Sunday, urging Israeli supporters to reinstate him as prime minister so the pair could "finish the job" in Iran.

"As everyone is aware, including the enemy, Bibi and I have had a great relationship in winning together," he said, referring to Netanyahu by a common nickname. In his post, Trump pointed to the U.S. and Israel's joint military operations in Iran, which he said had destroyed the country's military and economy.

"When you go to the Polls please remember that Bibi has been an outstanding Warrior Prime Minister!" he said, in comments directed at voters in Israel. "Vote for Bibi Netanyahu for Prime Minister, we have to finish the job that we started!"

Eurasia's Sabet told CNBC that the anti-Netanyahu bloc might be "more conciliatory on some issues," such as military action in Gaza, especially if doing so would improve U.S. ties and Israel's international standing while still meeting the country's basic security needs.

He said a government composed mostly of the anti-Netanyahu bloc would likely take fewer actions in the West Bank, crack down on settler violence against Palestinians there, and avoid annexation of Palestinian land.

The West Bank is a Palestinian territory west of the Jordan River where Israeli settlements have been expanding for decades. In recent years, violence and forced displacement of Palestinians by settlers have drawn condemnation from lawmakers in the U.S. and beyond.

But Sabet told CNBC: "While the opposition to Netanyahu has the edge in the latest Israeli election polls, this will be a tight race, with several possible outcomes."

#296. Chinese scientists discover “D-rex,” a giant fungus with roots stretching back 65 million years

📅 26 October 2026 | Sumber

Scientists exploring the forests of Yunnan, China, have discovered an extraordinary giant fungus that is challenging previous assumptions about how large certain fungi can grow. The newly identified species, Dianjunus rex, produces upright reproductive structures that can reach 50 cm (20 inches) in height and weigh as much as 2.2 kg (4.9 pounds). These are the largest known fruiting bodies among fungi belonging to the phylum Ascomycota.

"This remarkable species represents a new fungal family, Dianjunaceae, and provides a rare window into the evolution of extreme fungal body forms," said Dr Indunil C Senanayake, an associate professor at the Germplasm Bank of Wild Species of the Kunming Institute of Botany in China and corresponding author of the study, published in Frontiers in Fungal Biology.

"The discovery illustrates how much fungus biodiversity remains to be discovered in East Asian forests."

Researchers from the Kunming Institute of Botany encountered the unusual fungus while surveying several forest environments in Yunnan. Their fieldwork included temperate coniferous forests near Damaidi and Yipinglang, along with tropical rainforest near Nanbang.

The team spotted unusually large, whitish reproductive structures, known as 'stromata', growing from the woody roots of Chinese cork oak trees. These structures emerged from the rhizosphere, the region of soil surrounding plant roots, and appeared to belong to an unidentified member of the ascomycete fungi.

Ascomycetes make up the largest major group of fungi, with more than 64,000 recognized species. Unlike familiar mushrooms, these fungi do not produce true mushroom structures. Instead, they generate spores within tiny sac-like structures found inside or on the surfaces of their fruiting bodies.

To investigate the discovery, the scientists collected samples and preserved reference specimens in the Kunming Institute of Botany's collections. They also cultivated spores under laboratory conditions to examine the fungus's physical characteristics and sequenced its genome, including its protein-coding genes.

Meet D-Rex, a Record-Breaking Fungal Giant

The genetic analysis, together with a close examination of the fungus's physical features, revealed that the discovery represented much more than a previously unknown species. It was sufficiently different from known fungi to require the creation of a new genus and an entirely new family (Dianjunaceae) within the order Xylariales.

The researchers named the species Dianjunus rex, drawing inspiration from its impressive size and the ancient Dian kingdom. Its nickname, 'D-rex', reflects its exceptional stature among related fungi.

Its closest known relative is Graphostroma platystoma, a fungus that grows on dead hardwood throughout the Northern Hemisphere. That species is the sole representative of its own family, Graphostromataceae.

Members of the order Xylariales are known for producing a variety of specialized chemical compounds and enzymes capable of breaking down complex molecules in plants. Researchers believe similar enzymes may allow 'D-rex' to decompose dead wood and obtain nutrients from it.

A 65-Million-Year Connection to Dinosaur Extinction

One of the most intriguing findings concerns the ancient evolutionary origins of the newly identified fungal family.

Using a technique known as a 'molecular clock', the scientists compared the fungus's DNA with genomic information from hundreds of other fungi whose evolutionary histories have been established. This analysis allowed them to estimate when the Dianjunaceae family first appeared.

Their results suggest that the lineage originated approximately 65 million years ago, roughly one million years after the Cretaceous-Paleogene mass extinction. That catastrophic event eliminated the non-avian dinosaurs along with countless other animal and plant species.

The timing raises the possibility that the enormous environmental changes following the extinction helped create favorable conditions for the ancestors of this unusual fungus.

"This timing raises an intriguing possibility. After the mass extinction, forests experienced dramatic changes, including the sudden availability of large amounts of dead plant material," said Senanayake. "For wood-associated decomposing fungi, such environmental disruption may have created new ecological opportunities."

Another mystery is how and why Dianjunus rex evolved such an extraordinary size.

Before its discovery, the tallest known ascomycete fruiting bodies measured approximately 20 to 30 cm. The newly identified fungus can reach 50 cm, making it substantially taller than the previous record holders.

One possible explanation involves how the fungus releases and spreads its spores. By extending high above the forest floor, its reproductive structures may be better positioned to catch moving air and distribute spores through dense vegetation.

However, growing such a large structure also requires considerable energy. The researchers suggest that this unusual evolutionary strategy would be advantageous only in environments where the benefits of greater spore dispersal outweigh the resources needed for growth.

"A fruiting body which towers above surrounding vegetation and debris could have better dispersal of spores by wind in dense forests. However, such a large structure requires substantial energy investment, suggesting that this strategy likely evolved only where the ecological benefits outweighed the costs," hypothesized Senanayake.

China's Forests May Harbor More Undiscovered Fungi

The discovery also highlights how much remains unknown about fungal diversity in China's subtropical forests.

Researchers believe the region is particularly well suited to the evolution of unusual fungal species because it contains a wide variety of habitats, has experienced relatively stable climatic conditions, and supports intricate relationships among living organisms.

Despite these favorable conditions, many fungi in the region have received little scientific attention. Remote and difficult terrain complicates fieldwork, while the seasonal appearance and often hidden nature of fungal reproductive structures make some species especially difficult to locate. Historically, research has also concentrated heavily on fungi with commercial or practical value.

The scientists expect that continued exploration of these forests will uncover additional species, potentially revealing more unexpected forms and evolutionary histories.

"This region combines exceptional habitat heterogeneity, climatic stability, and complex biotic interactions that promote fungal diversification. Historically, however, fungal diversity in these ecosystems has been underestimated due to logistical difficulties in field sampling, the seasonal and cryptic nature of fungal fruiting, and a historical emphasis on economically important fungi," said Senanayake.

#298. Exclusive: From Pro Patria to the World: Estrella’s new model for running football clubs

📅 27 October 2026 | Sumber

This past July, Pro Patria became the first Italian club Estrella Football Group acquired: Football Italia sits down with Estrella's co-founder and President, David Dwinger, to learn more about the group's plans for the club and how the project reflects its wider vision for football.

Success in football can take many forms. It can mean lifting trophies on the pitch, building a sustainable club, or developing a thriving youth academy that nurtures the next generation of talent.

Coming from a family of Dutch champions and Olympians, David Dwinger understands the dedication and sacrifice required to compete at the highest level. Through Estrella Football Group, his goal is to create the environment and foundations that allow that potential to flourish.

In July, Estrella Football Group acquired Pro Patria, its third club after Portugal-based Cascais SAD and Carvoeiro United.

"We started off buying Cascais because it was just a childhood dream to have a football club," Dwinger says in an exclusive interview with Football Italia.

David Dwinger, Co-founder & President of Estrella Football Group, inside Pro Patria's stadium.

Estrella Football Group is a European football investment company developing a horizontal multi-club ownership model.

Rather than imposing a rigid hierarchy, the model lets clubs remain independent while benefiting from shared knowledge, operational resources, and long-term planning. The ultimate mission is to create an environment where their clubs can compete at a higher level while strengthening their foundations for long-term growth.

With a strong background in sport tech companies, David and Estrella Group have been looking for the next standard, the next club, since they bought Cascais in 2024.

"In digital worlds everything is scalable. You just add more servers, and you can scale to the next 100,000 customers. In football, that's different," he says.

When the company announced it was looking to buy another club after Cascais, about 100 signed up, so Estrella started to set its own criteria: "We started looking at the country, the city, the catchment area and of course, the finance, a big part of it," David says.

"Then the people who work there and the history. We effectively started building our first set of criteria, which I think now contains 45 criteria, and we built a tool.

"That's how we started gathering information," he continues.

"Currently, I think we have over 3,000 clubs in our tool. Predominantly from Europe. Predominantly from football countries. But Italy is a bigger football country than others, of course."

The process starts long before formal negotiations. When a club makes contact, Estrella Football Group analyses a wide range of available data using its proprietary platform. A strong overall assessment opens the door to more detailed discussions about a possible investment.

So, what stood out about Pro Patria, an Italian Serie D club based in Busto Arsizio, in the region of Lombardy?

"I really liked the history as well as the close proximity to Milan. There's, of course, a lot of football going on there," David says.

"I liked the context, which is very difficult as a criterion. But it's very important to us. So, the context, in this case, specifically of Luca Bassi, who is very important for us as a partner, because he's effectively our equal partner.

"He is from the city. He's very much emotionally attached to the club, and that brings a lot of value to us. We also see the potential there, and the infrastructure is quite good. The stadium may be a bit old, but there's room to grow.

David Dwinger, Co-founder & President of Estrella Football Group.

"It should be a Serie C club, of course. And we see the potential to bring it at least to Serie B. Probably not in the next two years. But it has that potential."

The Estrella Football Group has four macro-areas that describe the types of clubs they could acquire.

There are 'Brand clubs', where the location makes the difference: "Beautiful places, like where I am today," David says from his office in Cascais.

"Technically, this club can't get beyond the fourth division in the current location. So, that's a big issue. The reality is that I can't go beyond a certain level, but it will never lose the location or the name.

"Then we look at academy clubs, which are very strong for their youth departments," David continues.

"Then we look at performance clubs, which for us are the clubs which could have the potential to already be on a pro level, like Serie A, or Serie B.

"And then we look at fallen angels. They're closely related to performance clubs, used to be big clubs, and have been struggling over the last few years.

"Pro Patria, for me, sits between a performance club and an academy club."

And the academy focus should not be overlooked; quite the opposite. A key feature of Estrella Football Group, in fact, is the balance between collective support and local autonomy. On the one hand, clubs within the group share resources and best practices, but, locally, they continue to develop their own sporting project, keeping a strong connection with supporters and local communities.

"I feel that the academy is the base of a club. So, I think we need to have a strong academy with the potential to make these guys really become pro players," David says.

"In the end, that's what you dream of when you're a little boy, right? You like to play football. You like to play with your mates, train, have fun, and enjoy it.

"My son used to play at the Ajax academy and for me, that's the starting point. A club needs a strong academy to grow. Not every player will make it to the first team, but my ambition, and Estrella Football Club's, should be to achieve the highest growth from the academy to the first team.

"I think our clubs should be known for giving out youth contracts," he continues.

"I'd like to have it broader because I believe once we do that, it adds something to your club, to the infrastructure and, very importantly, to the scouting model. If you are known for that, then the scouting becomes inbound. So, we need to change that youth model, that academy model."

David Dwinger, Co-founder & President of Estrella Football Group.

Every city, every region, every country has its own story, but what challenges and opportunities does investing in Italian football present?

"Exceptions, of course, are everywhere, but I see a lot of Fallen Angels. It feels like a high percentage of clubs in Italy are Fallen Angels, maybe more than in the Netherlands or Spain. It feels like it, maybe because we look at Italy a lot.

"What I would really like to ensure is that clubs like Pro Patria, especially now that we're involved, become really stable and not opportunistic.

"There's a lot of culture, a lot of emotion. So we should build it up even more, right? Imagine showing movies on the pitch, like an open-air cinema, and that movie night also gives you a free ticket to the next match. Or organising gala dinners at the stadium.

"And we can build content around that, and that content allows us to attract more eyeballs and get people to buy shirts in countries which are maybe even close to Italy. It's exactly what's happening all year in Portugal. I truly feel we can do that because Pro Patria isn't coming from nothing, right?

"We need to win everything, sure. But then there's also realism and building a system that is sustainable, as self-sustainable as possible."

The project is about building a solid network and sharing expertise and opportunities, which will lead to success on the field. It's not about millions of euros in new signings.

"I want to build a system and a foundation which works to ensure that the club will be here for 100 more years. When we focus on the business side, it positively affects what's happening on the field.

"I want to be promoted, but not just for the sake of promotion. I want promotion because we've done everything well. And that should result in promotion.

"And that the business side and business intelligence and structures and frameworks all complement the drive to win. And actually, we've seen that work a couple of times now.

"I want to win. We're all entrepreneurs as well, so I'm always surrounded by people who want to win, but we want to work directly with the club's local teams, because that's where the local knowledge sits, the cultural understanding.

"Working with [Pro Patria President] Rosanna [Zema] and [Sporting director] Giovanni [Giovanditti], and then the new head of youth, Augusto [Splendore], and Luca [Bassi], who's based in London.

"We want to work with the local teams. We do that for all the clubs. And then we implement our tooling."

Each club works locally, but how do they share information and knowledge and, ultimately, help each other grow?

"We've built an application called ClubOS. It's an operating system for a football club," David says.

"It sits in every department, which we implement at all our clubs. External clients also use it. We've got a couple of pro clubs in the Netherlands using that tool, and we're now rolling it out for Europe.

"We've got a lot of ideas," David continues.

"We can do Estrella tournaments. The logical part is player training, player pathways, youth. But also from the staff perspective.

"For example, two years ago, the staff of Cascais went to Atletico Madrid for two days to work with their technical staff. And of course, Atletico is not an Estrella club, but it is a client of one of our applications. So that ecosystem, that network, is what we're always trying to optimise and implement.

David Dwinger inside the Pro Patria headquarters.

"There's a lot of knowledge per football club, which is within the walls of a football club and doesn't really get out. We want to optimise that knowledge within our clubs, not just dictate from our side.

"We have strong opinions on how to run a football club, but we miss the local details. So this is how we work together.

"I think it will be great to start setting up Estrella events where all the staff come together. One year we go to Pro Patria, the next year we go to a club in Portugal, and now we're working on a club in Austria and the UK. So that's all very specific knowledge with a lot of people with a lot of experience."

There are already projects taking shape, involving Pro Patria as well.

"These are very early conversations. But we are looking at the pitch at Pro Patria, which could use improvement. We are fairly closely connected to a very large Dutch company, TenCate, which creates pitches.

"They actually have a plant and a factory in Italy, so we're now in conversations with them on maybe starting a partnership with Estrella, so that all the Estrella clubs can get a great pitch from them.

"It's the same we've done with the ticketing system, or x the GPS system. These are all partners for Estrella."

A fairly small team runs all of Estrella's management. The daily work involves David's two ventures, founding partner Alessandro Nuccetelli, Estrella co-founder and CEO Xander Czaikowski, former CEO of PEC Zwolle in the Netherlands, and Global Sports Director Cristiano Piccini, a former Italy international and Valencia defender.

"We deliberately want to keep Estrella core team as small as possible. Because every euro I spend on a new guy is not going towards buying a football club," David concludes.

"Estrella's goal is to buy five clubs per year. We believe that with our horizontal MCO, we're the world's first horizontal MCO, and that if we put the clubs next to each other, rather than stacking them on top of each other, this one becomes less important than the top one. We want to do it like this. That means that with every club we add, we add something else to the flywheel."

#303. Oil Spills Wreak Havoc on the Bottom of the Ocean, Even a Decade Later

📅 25 October 2026 | Sumber

This story originally appeared on Inside Climate News and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

Across hundreds of miles of the northern Gulf of Mexico, a deepwater ecosystem collapsed after the massive 2011 Deepwater Horizon oil and gas spill, and recovery is uncertain, new research concludes.

The study, published Monday in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, found that animal populations—including octopus, krill, squid, and shrimp—declined by 60 to 85 percent in the three and a half years after the spill, with few signs of recovery since. Krill and lanternfish, both foundational species in the Gulf’s food web, were among the hardest hit. The findings also suggest that the die-off is causing genetic bottlenecks that could further hinder ecosystem recovery.

The researchers identified it as the “fastest and most severe faunal decline reported for Earth’s largest ecosystem type” ever documented. The widespread die-off of marine organisms may also reduce the ocean’s ability to transport carbon dioxide from the atmosphere to the deep sea. After ruling out other factors, such as water temperature and oxygen levels, the researchers identified the Deepwater Horizon blowout as “the most parsimonious explanation” for the ecosystem’s collapse.

Comprehensive natural resource damage assessments and restoration efforts involving federal, state, and tribal trustees are ongoing. In 2016, BP agreed to a $20.8 billion settlement, including up to $8.8 billion for environmental restoration.

Remote ocean depths and habitats miles below the surface may seem buffered from the impacts of human activity, the authors wrote, but their findings suggest an industrial disaster pushed part of it into a diminished state with “limited resilience to facilitate recovery.” They said their findings also show that proposed industrial deep-sea mining could damage the ecosystem before baseline conditions are assessed.

A transoceanic drilling rig, operating for BP about 50 miles southeast of the Mississippi Delta, exploded on April 20, 2010. The explosion and fire killed 11 people and triggered the largest accidental marine oil spill in history.

Oil and gas spewed uncontrollably from the broken well nearly a mile deep for 87 days, ejecting 4.9 million barrels of oil at a rate of about 400 tanker trucks per day, enough to fill up 1.2 million cars. The spill also released about 7.7 billion cubic feet of fossil gas into the deep sea at a rate of 88 million cubic feet per day, enough to supply about 820,000 US homes. State and federal agencies, including the Environmental Protection Agency, also authorized BP to apply 1.84 million gallons of chemical dispersants to try to reduce the impacts.

Some of the oil and gas dissipated and was transported out of the deep Gulf of Mexico region. Some coated barrier islands and devastated coastal wetlands and shellfish habitat, and some settled onto the ocean floor, where currents can stir it back into the water. But enough hydrocarbon and chemical-dispersant remnants stayed suspended long enough to do almost immeasurable harm.

A series of studies since the spill have shown a wide range of toxic effects on marine organisms, from impaired development and reproduction to increased mortality and lasting health problems in dolphins and whales. The new paper suggests that lingering pollutants may interfere with some species’ ability to find mates in the dark by disrupting their highly developed sense of smell.

The impacts continue to ripple through the ecosystem, said lead author Tracey Sutton, a professor of marine and environmental sciences at Nova Southeastern University in Florida. A 2024 study found an 80 percent decline in deep-diving toothed whales, he said.

“We used to have a big resident population of sperm whales right off the Mississippi River, but we haven’t seen a sperm whale in 10 years,” he said. Large predators need big, occasional dense patches of prey, and those have disappeared, he added.

Scientists have developed accurate ways to count fish. For this study, they started with a baseline from nine months of sampling in 2011 and compared it with nine subsequent surveys between 2015 and 2023. The researchers sampled deep-pelagic habitat along a large grid around the spill site from about 650 feet below the surface to about a mile down. The deep-pelagic zone accounts for about 90 percent of the Gulf’s total volume.

Across a grid of stations, scientists on slippery decks lowered and hoisted nets that open and close at different depths, with experts from different species groups to identify the catch. They sampled around noon and midnight to account for species that migrate vertically each day. Ship-mounted scientific echosounders provided an independent check, measuring sound reflected by marine life in the water column.

The research is “comprehensive and carefully composed,” marine biologist Bruce Robison, a senior scientist at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute, said via email. “There is no other study that I know of with such an incredible number of net samples,” added Robison, who did not participate in the new study.

The research focuses on species that are not commercially fished and shows for the first time that human impacts can deplete marine life even in very deep ocean water, he said.

“It is important for the public to understand just how disastrous this oil spill was,” Robison said. “The Gulf has not recovered, and it’s been over 15 years.” Robison said other activities, such as deep-sea mining, could also have severe negative consequences for deepwater pelagic ecosystems by discharging wastewater containing metals or lubricants.

Three lines of evidence—net hauls, acoustic surveys, and genetic sampling—corroborate each other, which is “unusually strong evidence to support his conclusions,” said Jeffrey Drazen, a marine ecologist at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, who did not participate in the new study.

The study examines all possible causes of the decline and shows only one aligns with the scientific evidence, he said.

“Through logical elimination,” he said, “and without actually pointing a finger, they leave no doubt that the oil spill is the cause of the decline.”

#304. India slashes cost of cancer drugs after court rules mark-ups are ‘extortion’

📅 23 October 2026 | Sumber

Case filed in 2022 by patient unable to afford medicine leads to cap on drug prices for millions who face ruin if diagnosed

The Indian government has moved to reduce the price of cancer drugs after a retired bank clerk took her case to the supreme court.

From next month, 137 cancer drugs in India will be cheaper as the government tries to tackle the tragedy of poorer patients either forgoing treatment, selling land or falling into debt to meet the high cost of some medicines, which are making large profits for hospitals and pharmacists.

Sarojam Radhakrishnan, a former bank employee in Kerala, was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2021. Doctors prescribed life-saving targeted treatments but the monthly cost, of more than 63,000 rupees (£500), was far beyond her family’s means.

Realising that thousands of families were being ruined by the cost of such drugs, Radhakrishnan filed a petition to the Kerala high court in 2022 demanding government intervention to lower the costs.

When the case reached the supreme court, the judges looked at hospitals’ and retailers’ mark-ups on cancer drugs and called the situation “carnage” and “extortion”.

During a hearing on 29 September, justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta noted how a life-saving cancer drug supplied to hospitals at 2,700 rupees carried a vastly marked-up price of 27,000 rupees.

The judges found that hospitals, distributors and chemists enjoyed large margins on medicines. Analysis by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority revealed a trade mark-up on some cancer drugs averaging 170%, with some extreme examples stretching to more than 700%.

A 30% trade margin cap on the price of 42 drugs has been in place for some years but many others remained off this list. Now, prodded by the supreme court’s findings, the government has imposed the cap on 137 other drugs.

“The measure is expected to reduce medicine prices by up to 70% and help cancer patients save 2,500 crore rupees [£199m] annually, significantly reducing the amount they pay from their own pockets,” a statement from the Department of Pharmaceuticals said.

People on low incomes in India dread illness, as the cost of treatment can mean financial ruin, particularly for cancer patients.

Whenever the Indian Cancer Society holds a free diagnosis camp in Gurgaon where he lives, Krishan Kalra urges local drivers, maids, cooks and tailors to turn up because tests they cannot afford are offered free.

As a former member of the council of the Rajiv Gandhi Cancer Institute and Research Centre, Kalra knows the importance of early diagnosis, but he said very few people attended. “When I ask why, they say they’re too scared – if something serious like cancer is detected, they haven’t got the money to pay for the treatment so they prefer to remain in the dark,” he said.

With the cost of cancer drugs ranging in price from 38,000 to 380,000 rupees, many families quietly walk out of the doctor’s consulting room upon hearing the estimated cost of treatment.

Studies by the Public Health Foundation of India show that spending on healthcare pushes about 55 million Indians a year below the poverty line.

Few Indians can afford the premiums for comprehensive health insurance. The government’s nationwide insurance scheme, Ayushman Bharat, covers treatment for some cancers but it provides only 500,000 rupees’ worth of annual cover for a family – the cost of just one dose of Kadcyla (ado-trastuzumab emtansine), a drug used to treat breast cancer. Patients may need up to 14 doses.

Dr Ravi Kannan is a surgical oncologist and director of Cachar cancer hospital and research centre in Silchar, Assam. He has worked in hospitals elsewhere in India and is familiar with doctors’ trauma of seeing patients walk out to go home and die.

“Some families start the treatment, hoping against hope to manage the cost. They start but they don’t come back for chemotherapy or radiation. They can’t sustain the cost,” he said. “The decision is a welcome step if the outcome is that more patients can access the drugs they need.”

India records about 1.56m new cancer cases annually – up from 1.39m cases in 2020 – making it a significant public health challenge.

As the supreme court delves deeper into the subject, what was clear, said Jyotsna Singh, co-convener of the Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatments, a civil society network, was that a “total overhaul” of the healthcare system was needed.

“Right from the cost of manufacturing a drug to the point of sale, we need to make the system transparent and regulate the entire supply chain. Only then will these drugs become available to those who need them,” she said.

Singh said companies and hospitals were likely to try to find legal loopholes to wriggle out of the 30% cap, suggesting that hospitals may offset the lower price charged for a drug by raising charges on other items.

The supreme court judges have also asked the government’s lawyers why the cap should apply only to cancer drugs and not the entire range of non-patented drugs. The court has given the government until 27 October to respond.

Unfortunately, the court’s ruling came too late for Radhakrishnan, who died in September 2022 while her case was still pending in Kerala.

#305. Millennials and Gen Z are excitedly buying Lego, plushies, and other toys. It's becoming big business.

📅 27 October 2026 | Sumber

As a child, you may have sung along to Toys R Us' iconic jingle about not wanting to grow up. Decades later, many millennial and Gen Z adults are taking that motto seriously.

Adults are rediscovering how Lego, stuffed animals, and other toys brought them joy. Now that they're earning their own money, they can afford the things they once played with or circled in catalogs. Hobby spending — which includes hobby shops, arts and crafts stores, and outdoor recreation providers — rose 7.9% year over year in August, according to an analysis by the Bank of America Institute.

Devin Byron, 25, had a collection of American Girl dolls growing up, but her interest in playing with them fizzled out around middle school. However, her love for them never really went away. And now, working an office job, she can buy her own.

In February, she and her friend went to the American Girl store in New York. Byron purchased the historical doll representing the '60s, Melody, which cost $135 with the book, plus $34 for accessories.

"I feel like a lot of collectors now are, I would say, healing their inner child because some people couldn't get maybe American Girl dolls growing up, but now they can," Byron said. "And it's an adrenaline rush too."

She's not the only adult contributing to the toy economy. Market research company Circana found that adult-only households made up over half of toy sales in the first half of this year, and that overall toy sales for adults increased 25%. Some adults may buy toys to bring nostalgia back into their lives or to avoid doomscrolling. For others, it's to make a profit.

"We're seeing toys increasingly function as hobbies, fandom ecosystems, and social experiences rather than traditional children's products," said Kristen McLean, vice president of client insights for Circana's Entertainment Knowledge Group. "That's expanding the consumer base and creating new opportunities for manufacturers and retailers that understand how to engage collectors, enthusiasts, gifters, and self-purchasers."

Jay Berino, store manager at the Lowry Town Center Timbuk Toys in Denver, pointed to "kidulting," the trend in which adults engage with childlike toys and hobbies, as coming from adults seeking distractions and nostalgia — from buying Pokémon cards to lava lamps.

"As much as we're a toy store and people hear toy store and think of kids, we sell to a lot to full-blown adults, and that drives a huge chunk of our business," he said.

Syls Farmer, 32, runs a vintage online store specializing in toys marketed to girls. Her store, Mema's Doll Shop, was inspired by her grandmother, who ran a couple of toy stores back in the day. Farmer said adults buy from her for themselves or for their kids so they can experience their past.

"A lot of people are dealing with a lot of pressure in this general economy and the world in general," Farmer said. "And I think that these items of childhood are bringing back feelings of comfort and peace that I think a lot of us need right now."

Farmer also buys toys for herself, including her first American Girl doll through Facebook Marketplace — Nicki, one of the '90s-inspired dolls.

Even crafters are getting in on the toy craze: Abby Glassenberg, the president of the Craft Industry Alliance, said that homemade Labubu-esque bag charms have taken off, with crafters making their own customizable charms from crochet or felt.

"People are definitely still spending. I think craft in some ways is resistant to market up and down," Glassenberg said. When the market is up, people pour more money into their hobbies, whether that's getting premium materials or even traveling to somewhere catered to their favorite crafts.

"When the market is down, and people's budgets are tighter, they want to make something for a gift rather than buy it," Glassenberg said.

Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.

Emma Wynn, 28, has 120 Jellycat items, a popular stuffed-toy brand that includes animals, food, and more. Wynn's collection began when she bought a scuba diver egg while browsing at a garden center with her family, sparking a feeling of childlike happiness.

Prices range on the Jellycat site; for instance, a heart dragon is priced at $80, a carrot cake is priced at $45, and bear winter decorations are priced at $28. Wynn funds her collection with money she earns from content creation, rather than from her corporate job.

Wynn thinks adults buy toys because they bring back happy childhood memories, can provide a dopamine hit when someone finds something they've been searching for a while, and can connect them with others who are building similar collections.

"It feels very empowering to be unapologetic about the things that bring us joy and happiness, whereas before maybe I would've been embarrassed about it," she said.

It can also be a tangible way to remember a memory. For instance, Wynn's soon-to-be mother-in-law bought her a Jellycat flower bouquet to celebrate her new engagement.

Harrison Woodward, 28, said building and playing with Lego sets was a large part of his childhood. For one birthday in his early 20s, his aunt bought him a Lego Porsche car model, reigniting his passion for Lego sets. He put on a streaming show after a long day of work and started to build the over 1,000-piece product.

"It was just the most therapeutic, peaceful activity," he said. "You could sit there for a few hours, a few days in a row, and complete a set and see it come together and marvel at all the different engineering things that they put into these sets now."

He left his job in insurance to focus on content creation full time. He posts about his Lego collection and passion for cars; he recently started collecting Hot Wheels, another childhood favorite. He has spent thousands on Lego and is running out of space in a room that's filled with his collections. He still tries to find a balance so that building isn't just for content, such as taking his time to build a CaDA car set in the evening.

Woodward thinks adults might be purchasing toys to invest some time in their hobbies and take care of their mental health.

"I think the stigma has kind of lifted over collecting and everything," he said. "I think that for a long time people thought any of this stuff was strictly for kids, but as the years have gone on and adults have continued to adopt it, the stigma continues to go further and further away."

Trading cards have also become a major area of interest for some adults. Kian Golshan previously told Business Insider that Pokémon is a lucrative side hustle. For instance, he sold a Japanese-edition Charmander for $750 that he bought for $59.26. As Business Insider's Samuel O'Brient previously reported, Golshan was able to put the analytical skills that he developed while working in finance to work.

"It helps me kind of think through the risks and when to take profits, when to sell, what to hold, what's my like risk profile, what's tracking the market," Golshan said.

Byron, the Gen Zer who bought an American doll, still has her collection of dolls from her childhood. Plus, she has her most recent addition displayed in her room.

"I'm actually thinking about going back to the store again," she said. "Maybe I'll walk out with another doll. I guess we'll see."

#306. AI detects “invisible” signs of pancreatic cancer years before diagnosis

📅 26 October 2026 | Sumber

An artificial intelligence model called REDMOD can identify extremely subtle changes in pancreatic tissue that may signal cancer long before the disease becomes visible to doctors or conventional imaging technology. According to research published online in the journal Gut, the system can detect early signs of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, the most common type of pancreatic cancer.

Researchers believe this technology could help transform pancreatic cancer detection by identifying the disease at a much earlier stage (stage 0), when treatment is more likely to succeed. Instead of receiving a diagnosis after the cancer has progressed to an advanced, potentially terminal stage, patients might have an opportunity to begin treatment while the disease is still treatable.

Although REDMOD outperformed experienced radiologists in the study, more research is necessary before it can be introduced into routine medical care. In particular, the scientists emphasize the need to test the system in patients at high risk, including those experiencing unexplained weight loss or recently diagnosed diabetes.

Why Pancreatic Cancer Is So Difficult to Detect Early

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma has a low survival rate, largely because it is often discovered only after the disease has advanced. Early pancreatic cancer typically produces few noticeable symptoms, and the changes it causes in pancreatic tissue can be too subtle to detect through standard medical imaging. The cancer can also progress rapidly, making timely diagnosis especially important.

To address these challenges, researchers created an artificial intelligence framework known as Radiomics-based Early Detection MODel (REDMOD). The system analyzes extremely fine patterns in the texture of pancreatic tissue, known as radiomics (radiomics), that are not readily visible on conventional computed tomography (CT) scans.

REDMOD also automatically identifies and outlines the pancreas, separating it from nearby organs and tissues. This process eliminates the need for specialists to manually trace the organ's boundaries, reducing the inconsistencies that can arise when different people perform the task.

AI Finds Hidden Cancer Signals Years Before Diagnosis

To evaluate the system, the researchers examined abdominal CT scans from 219 patients treated at multiple hospitals. At the time of their scans, experienced radiologists had found no evidence of pancreatic cancer. However, every patient in this group was subsequently diagnosed with the disease.

The scans had been taken at different intervals before diagnosis. For 87 patients (40%), the images were obtained 3 to 12 months earlier. Another 76 patients (35%) had been scanned 12 to 24 months before diagnosis, while 56 (25%) had undergone imaging more than 24 months earlier (up to around 3 years). In nearly two thirds (64%) of the patients, the cancer developed in the head of the pancreas.

The researchers compared these images with CT scans from 1243 people who remained free of pancreatic cancer for up to three years afterward. The comparison group was matched according to age, sex, and the dates of their scans.

Patients who eventually developed pancreatic cancer had an average age of 69, with ages ranging from 34 to 88. Those in the comparison group were 64 years old on average, with the same age range of 34 to 88.

REDMOD successfully identified subtle imaging signatures associated with pancreatic cancer an average of 475 days before patients received their clinical diagnoses. These early warning signs had previously gone undetected during routine radiological assessments.

"This temporal window holds profound significance, as attaining such early detection would substantially augment the probability of cure and improved survival," highlight the researchers.

"In fact, modelling studies indicate that increasing the proportion of localized [pancreatic ductal carcinomas] from 10% to 50% would more than double survival rates, thereby underscoring that the timing of diagnosis is the single most critical determinant of survival outcomes," they add.

The results also showed that REDMOD was substantially better than experienced radiologists at recognizing early cancer signals.

The AI achieved a sensitivity of 73%, compared with 39% for radiologists. Sensitivity measures how effectively a diagnostic method identifies people who actually have the disease, rather than overlooking genuine cases.

The difference was even more pronounced when researchers examined scans taken more than two years before the patients were diagnosed. In these cases, REDMOD achieved a detection rate of 68%, nearly three times the 23% recorded by radiologists.

The researchers also assessed how well the system could recognize scans from people without pancreatic cancer. In an independent group of 539 patients from several hospitals, REDMOD correctly classified just over 81% of scans as cancer free. It performed even better on the publicly available US National Institutes of Health NIH-PCT dataset (80 patients), correctly identifying 87.5% as free of pancreatic cancer.

Additional testing suggested that the early warning signs detected by REDMOD were consistent over time. When the researchers analyzed scans taken from the same patients several months apart, the system produced matching results in 90 to 92% of cases. This consistency strengthened the evidence that the AI was identifying meaningful changes associated with the disease.

Could AI Transform Early Pancreatic Cancer Detection?

Despite the promising findings, the researchers caution that several questions remain unanswered. One limitation is that the study population did not include a sufficiently diverse range of ethnic backgrounds, which could affect how well the technology performs across different populations.

The system must also undergo prospective testing, particularly among people at increased risk of pancreatic cancer, before researchers can determine whether it will be effective in everyday clinical practice.

Even with these limitations, the findings suggest that AI could eventually help doctors identify pancreatic cancer while it is still at a much more treatable stage, potentially improving survival for patients who would otherwise receive a late diagnosis.

The researchers conclude: "This study validates REDMOD as a fully automated AI framework capable of identifying the imaging signatures of stage 0 [pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma] in normal pancreas, achieving this with substantial lead times and performance superior to expert radiologists."

They add: "While prospective validation is paramount to confirm clinical utility, the REDMOD framework represents a significant advance towards shifting the paradigm for sporadic [pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma] from a late-stage symptomatic diagnosis to proactive pre-clinical interception, offering tangible hope for improving outcomes in this challenging disease."

#307. Inherited IRAs can boost wealth — and trigger a tax bill. Here's how to reduce it

📅 27 October 2026 | Sumber

An inherited individual retirement account can be a sizable windfall for some investors — but taxes can take a chunk without proper planning, experts say.

On average, heirs receive inherited IRAs at age 59, and the mean balance of those accounts is $128,000, according to a recent Vanguard report that analyzed nearly 83,000 accounts in 2024.

"Most people inherit an IRA in their 50s, right at the peak of their earning years, and then have to empty it within 10 years," said certified financial planner Michael Walstedt, founding advisor of Reliant Wealth Advisory in Hoboken, New Jersey.

Since 2020, a "10-year rule" applies to some inherited accounts, requiring certain heirs, including adult children, to generally empty the balance by the 10th year after the original account owner's death.

If it's a pretax inherited IRA, the 10-year withdrawal timeline can boost adjusted gross income, potentially triggering higher taxes and reducing eligibility for other tax breaks, experts say.

Inherited IRA planning will continue to be important amid the so-called "great wealth transfer," with baby boomers expected to pass trillions of dollars to Gen Xers and millennials in the coming decades.

Over the next 20 to 25 years, total transfers between generations could be an estimated $74 trillion, according to a 2025 report from financial services firm UBS.

Whether you're preparing to leave a future gift or to inherit an IRA, there are some key tax moves to consider, financial experts say.

Since 2025, some adult children who receive an inherited IRA generally must start taking required minimum distributions, or RMDs, over the 10-year period or face an IRS penalty. The yearly RMD requirement applies if the original IRA owner reached RMD age, usually 73, before their death.

But even without yearly RMDs over the 10-year period, experts say, heirs should have a plan for pretax inherited accounts. Otherwise, they may have to take a large distribution in the 10th year, which could trigger a bigger-than-expected tax bill.

"I recommend projecting income over those 10 years and planning withdrawals around it," said CFP James Mayo, founder of IronFjord Wealth Management in Lakewood, Colorado.

For example, if you're expecting lower-income years due to retirement or a sabbatical, you could be in a lower tax bracket during those periods. Those years could be an opportunity to take bigger IRA distributions, he said.

Original account owners should also consider each heir's income tax bracket when choosing IRA beneficiaries, said certified public accountant Tim Steffen, director of advanced planning at financial services firm Baird.

For example, if one child is a law firm partner and the other is a teacher, "their incomes are wildly different," he said.

In that scenario, you might leave more of your IRA to the teacher because they'll pay less income tax, and you might leave a tax-free life insurance policy to the higher-earning attorney, Steffen said.

"Be more thoughtful about who actually inherits what, instead of just saying everybody gets an equal share of everything," he said.

If you're the original account owner, Roth IRA conversions during life "can make a big difference" for heirs, according to CFP Dinon Hughes, a partner with Nvest Financial in Portsmouth, New Hampshire.

Roth conversions transfer pretax or nondeductible IRA funds into a Roth IRA, which begins tax-free growth. The move triggers higher income in the year of the conversion, but could provide future heirs with more tax-free funds, experts say.

While certain inherited Roth IRAs are still subject to the 10-year rule, beneficiaries can generally withdraw the proceeds tax-free.

"The sweet spot for Roth conversions" is typically early retirement years, because income is lower before Social Security payments start and required minimum distributions kick in, Hughes said.

However, you'll need tax projections to see how extra income could affect other tax breaks, such as the $6,000 senior "bonus" deduction.

Plus, boosting adjusted gross income can affect income-related monthly adjustment amounts, or IRMAAs, which increase Medicare Part B and Part D premiums once income exceeds a certain level.

#309. Is PHP Running on Your ColdFusion Server? How to Check, and Remove It

📅 26 October 2026 | Sumber

If you run ColdFusion or Lucee on a Windows server with IIS, and you've never installed PHP on purpose, this one's for you. There's a good chance PHP is on your server. It may be left behind by a control panel, a phpMyAdmin install from years ago, or your host's setup image. Here's how to find out in a few minutes with PowerShell, and how to remove it safely if nothing uses it.

I remember when I could go years without applying a security fix. Now it feels like I'm chasing something down every few weeks: a patch here, a mitigation there, a bot hammering a page that shouldn't exist. Such is life in the AI era, sigh.

While I was signing in to my test blog the other day, the admin page refused me with a plain IIS error: 403 Forbidden, and a message saying multipart form-data requests were blocked by a PHP mitigation. My blogs are ColdFusion. They don't run a single line of PHP. So why was a PHP security rule stopping me from signing in?

The timing wasn't a coincidence. On October 21, 2026, PHP shipped emergency patches for two critical flaws that let an unauthenticated request run code on the server, nicknamed PHP2Shell. Every PHP setup that serves web requests was affected: PHP-FPM, Apache's mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. The fix is to install a new version of PHP (8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35).

My hosting company responded the same week with a web server security rule. The rule lived in IIS's server-wide URL Rewrite rules, so it applied to every site on the server and blocked every request whose content type was multipart/form-data, regardless of the address. That's the encoding a browser uses for any form that can upload a file, and plenty of forms use it even when they don't.

PHP's own advice doesn't include blocking those requests. It's to patch, and until then to turn off session.upload_progress.enabled and lower post_max_size. Several of the official mitigations concern how PHP handles uploads, so I can see why a host would reach for the biggest hammer. For a PHP site that's a blunt but understandable shield. For my ColdFusion sites it meant the admin sign-in form, every image upload and every file upload failed on all four sites at once. The rule matched every address, not just .php ones.

Once I'd scoped the rule to .php addresses (more on that below), everything worked again. Then I asked the obvious question: why is PHP on this server at all? The answer was a phpMyAdmin install I had asked for years ago to manage one MySQL database. It was still there, still in a site folder, and its login page was open to the whole internet. The host turned the blanket rule off once I told them PHP was no longer in use, and I went looking for anything else PHP had left behind.

IIS only runs PHP if a handler mapping tells it to. Open PowerShell as Administrator on the server:

If it prints nothing, IIS doesn't run PHP. If it prints something like this, it does, for every site that inherits the server's settings:

Note the handler's name and the scriptProcessor path. You'll need both if you remove it.

PowerShell's Get-ChildItem -Recurse works, but on a server with years of uploaded images it can crawl for minutes. Windows' own dir is much faster. This counts the PHP files under your web root:

If the count isn't zero, this shows which folders they're in, busiest first:

Mine found about 4,500 files in two folders, both phpMyAdmin: one inside a site, and a second copy at the web root, which IIS's Default Web Site served to anyone who visited the server's bare IP address.

If you find PHP files you don't recognize, especially scattered through image or upload folders, or changed recently, stop and treat it as a possible break-in. Attackers love dropping small PHP "web shells" into upload folders. This lists the most recently changed ones:

No php-cgi.exe process just means nothing has asked for a PHP page recently. IIS starts it on demand. The handler from Check 1 is what matters.

From any computer, try the usual addresses on your own sites:

Anything that answers 200 deserves a look. A phpMyAdmin login page facing the internet is a standing invitation: bots try passwords on it all day, and every attempt starts PHP and talks to your database.

Do these in order, and back up first. Every step is reversible.

IIS can snapshot its own configuration and restore it in one command:

To undo everything below: appcmd.exe restore backup "before-php-removal".

Move, don't delete. Its configuration file may hold a database password, so keep it somewhere private for a few weeks in case something turns out to need it:

If Move-Item complains that a file is in use, PHP has it open. iisreset /stop, move it, then iisreset /start. (Your sites are down for a few seconds.) And if it says "Could not find a part of the path", it's the destination folder that's missing, not the source. That one fooled me.

For managing MySQL afterwards, a desktop tool on the server over Remote Desktop, like HeidiSQL or MySQL Workbench, does everything phpMyAdmin did without a public login page.

IIS's request filtering can turn away a file extension before any handler sees it. Added at the server level, it covers every site:

Now any .php address gets "404 - the request filtering module is configured to deny the file extension", whether the file exists or not.

Use the handler name from Check 1 (mine was FastCGI) and the php-cgi.exe path:

Run Check 1 again. It should print nothing.

If PHP came from an installer, remove it under Apps > Installed apps. If it's just a folder like C:\php, rename it to C:\php-removed for a few weeks before deleting it. If anything complains, you'll know right away, and it's one rename to put back.

If PHP was installed by your host, ask them before step 5. Their own monitoring scripts are unlikely to need it, but it's their install.

Maybe you do run PHP somewhere, or your host wants their rule. Then scope it to PHP addresses instead of every address. The rule's was the whole problem. This changes it to .php addresses only, leaving ColdFusion's forms alone (use the rule's own name):

Note the single quotes around the pattern. I first tried the same change with appcmd.exe, and PowerShell quietly mangled the quoting: no error, and no change either. Set-WebConfigurationProperty with single quotes did it on the first try. Check the result with Select-String on C:\Windows\System32\inetsrv\config\applicationHost.config.

On Debian and Ubuntu, sudo a2dismod php8.3 (your version) and sudo systemctl restart apache2 stop Apache from running PHP. Then remove the packages with your package manager once you're sure nothing needs them. Control panels such as Virtualmin often install PHP for their own tools, so check before uninstalling.
