#315. Aung San Suu Kyi’s son speaks to detained former Myanmar leader for first time in five years

📅 22 October 2026 | Sumber

Kim Aris says ‘hearing her voice again means more than words can express’ amid loosening of detention restrictions

The son of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi has been allowed to speak to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years.

“Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris said in a post on Facebook on Thursday.

Aung San Suu Kyi is under house arrest in the capital, Naypyidaw, according to Myanmar authorities, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.

Images accompanying his Facebook post appeared to show Aris, who lives in the UK, standing outside the Myanmar embassy in London.

“I am deeply grateful to everyone who has stood by my mother and me. I believe your voices helped make this moment possible,” he said in the post. “But my mother is 81 and remains unjustly detained. One conversation is not regular family access.”

Myanmar’s military has held the Nobel peace prize laureate in almost total seclusion since the February 2021 coup, which ended a tentative decade-long experiment with democracy. But in recent months authorities have increasingly advertised the loosening of her detention and published photographs of her taking private meetings, as supporters have demanded “proof of life”.

On Monday, authorities said she received a package from Britain’s King Charles, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch. Buckingham Palace did not comment on the contents of the communication.

Myanmar authorities said Aung San Suu Kyi was moved from a prison in Naypyidaw to house arrest in April, and in August they published images of her meeting the nation’s Red Cross representative.

After ruling Myanmar as military chief since the coup, Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president this year.

Analysts described the election that put him in office as a charade, and said he could be loosening restrictions on Aung San Suu Kyi in an attempt to court international legitimacy.

#317. Historical Telecommunications

📅 14 February 2026 | Sumber

We're a loose collective of fairly technical people with an interest in historical telecommunications.

There is [so far] no legal entity behind this effort; it's just the collaboration of various individuals with a common goal. We spend our own money on acquiring historical artifacts and invest our spare time in documenting, repairing and researching them.

Most [large, public] telecommunications museums are rather disappointing from our view, as they are way too superficial and often happy with exhibiting some dead piece of hardware with a one-page description. What we are missing in many museums is equipment that is operational, as well as deeper knowledge about the context in which it was built, its internal operation, the major components it uses, the full user manuals, etc.

Furthermore, many communications museums focus on more early forms of electronic communications in the sense of analog telephony networks, electromechanical switching, telephones, telegraphs, etc. - while our main focus is more on the digital communications technology, roughly from the late 1960s through the late 1990s.

Our goals (and activities to reach those goals) are to

assemble, digitize, archive and publish information about historical [digital] telecommunications technologies, including

data sheets, user manuals, service manuals, schematics, firmware updates, etc. for end-user, network-side transmission and switching equipment

historical journals, books, articles, brochures and magazines about the respective technologies

collect, document, maintain, operate and exhibit historical [digital] telecommunications equipment

take high-resolution images of the equipment (both exterior and of all circuit boards) and publish them online

exhibit some of the equipment at certain events like vintage computing fairs/festivals or hacker conferences

develop, build and operate emulators for historical telecommunications networks to enable interested parties to operate their historical equipment against a simulated network over the internet

provide places online (such as chat, forum, mailing lists, video conferences) by which interested people can get in touch and collaborate within the goals of our project.

Areas of interest include (but are not limited to):

PCM (Pulse Code Modulation) transmission technology

CSPDNs (Circuit-Switched Public Data Networks) like German Datex-L

PSPDNs (Packet-Switched Public Data Networks) based on X.25 like German Datex-P

ISDN (Integrated Services Digital Network)

Digital Telephone Switching (EWSD, System 12, System X, AXE, ...)

#318. Indian court orders release of two leaders of Cockroach movement

📅 21 October 2026 | Sumber

Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in jail after defying restrictions on protests in Delhi amid government crackdown

An Indian court has ordered the release of two leaders of India’s Cockroach movement who were jailed last week amid a mounting state crackdown on youth-led protests.

The two leaders of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) movement, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, had spent a week in Delhi’s Tihar jail after being arrested by Delhi police last week.

On Wednesday, a special magistrate ordered that Das and Ranka be released, despite efforts by police to keep them in prison. They were made to sign a bond pledging no further breach of peace.

Their arrest came after a draconian police crackdown on a CJP march held in the capital two weeks ago to protest alleged manipulation of the country’s electoral roll, which led to the barricading of central Delhi and thousands of young people being detained.

Das and Ranka were taken into custody for a second time days later after they jumped police barricades and held up an Indian flag at a site in central Delhi that police had cordoned off.

The pair were charged with trespass and violating the peace and sent to jail for five days, which was then extended by two further days. Their detention had provoked outrage among leaders and supporters of the youth movement, who accused the government of “cowardice” for jailing CJP leaders for holding a peaceful protest.

After the magistrate’s ruling on Wednesday evening, Das said that “truth has triumphed”.

The release of the two leaders is likely to come as a blow to the ruling Narendra Modi government, which has implemented an unforgiving crackdown on recent protests that have erupted across India.

The CJP, alongside the opposition alliance, student groups and civil society, have been calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of the electoral roll that benefits Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) and has led to more than 130 million names being deleted from the voter register. The BJP has denied any interference.

The CJP began as an online satire earlier this year, but has since grown into a fully fledged political movement, challenging the powerful Modi government. Over the summer, it was Cockroach-led protests that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister after sustained demonstrations.

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the CJP movement, vowed over the weekend that the Modi regime and threat of jail would not intimidate the Cockroaches. Dipke was also detained on Friday after he called for a peaceful demonstration in central Delhi where CJP supporters would gather and wave the Indian flag in solidarity with Das and Ranka.

He had said that, once his fellow Cockroach leaders were released, they would “gather, re-strategise, and determine how to move forward”.

“The illegal arrests and detentions we have witnessed over the past few days indicate an attempt to intimidate us,” said Dipke. “But we will not be cowed down or retreat. This is a long battle and we are prepared for it.”

#319. Hyve Smart Package Locker Review: Protecting Your Holiday Deliveries

📅 25 October 2026 | Sumber

The onslaught of tech gear being delivered for WIRED Reviews, combined with the samples I receive constantly for my side hustle at Drinkhacker, means that delivery trucks are a constant occurrence on my suburban street. UPS and FedEx both make drops at my house nearly every day, and that’s not to mention occasional deliveries from the likes of DHL and, of course, Amazon and its ilk. But it’s usually not a problem. I work from home, so picking up packages left on the doorstep is just part of the scenery.

What is a problem is that I can’t be home 24 hours a day, and even though I have a very kind neighbor across the way who keeps an eye out for boxes on my front steps when I’m traveling, he isn’t always at home either. Package hold requests aren’t consistently honored by either of the major carriers—and earlier this year, FedEx seemingly discontinued its vacation hold option without bothering to tell anyone, the modern epidemic of porch piracy be damned. (A rep has since confirmed this with me, though no formal announcement has ever been made.)

Having packages held at shipping centers or access points usually costs money, typically about $5 per package and often more depending on the length of the hold, and that involves a trip after I get home to collect what’s arrived. If I’m gone for a week, that can mean fetching a dozen boxes or more.

All of that is a time-consuming pain, for which a startup called Hyve has come along to offer an assuagement: A smart lockbox that lets delivery drivers drop off packages in a secure location, notifying the homeowner whenever it’s been accessed. While the growing pains were significant, after weeks of testing, I found it a useful device that—just maybe—may earn a permanent home on my front porch.

Parcel lockboxes aren’t exactly a new concept. They operate basically like a standard post office mailbox, with a cantilevered hatch up top that allows deliveries to drop into a secure storage area below, where they can only be accessed through a keyed door. Delivery folks can put packages in through the hatch, but only you can get them out.

The Hyve Smart Package Locker is a play on this idea, forgoing the two-chamber design in favor of an electronic hatch accessed via 4-digit PINs. The box itself measures 32 inches high, 20 inches wide, and 20 inches deep, with interior dimensions about 4 inches shorter in each direction. That makes for a total of 7.4 cubic feet, which Hyve says will fit 80 percent of Amazon package sizes (though obviously this depends on the specifics of your ordering habits). For me, that math worked out: Deliveries of three-pack bottles of wine fit fine, but anything larger was typically left out by the courier.

It’s built from a combination of plastic and steel, and while the side panels seem a little flimsy, there’s enough reinforcement behind them that I never worried that the unit would be easily damaged by a would-be package thief without power tools. Units are available in gray or white; I requested the latter to match my home’s color, but alas received a gray one.

Assembly is required—and be warned, it’s no cakewalk. The locker comes packed flat, notably with no printed instructions on how to put all the pieces together. A QR code in the box takes you to a web page featuring a walkthrough video and a PDF guide, which are my two least favorite ways to be guided through an installation process on a cell phone. The PDF is very difficult to read on a small screen, and this contributed to making what was already a cumbersome construction process even more difficult. I consider myself quite handy, but I ultimately spent nearly an hour putting the locker together due to a couple of easy-to-overlook goofs. Real, printed instructions—especially considering they’re all of five pages long—would go a long way toward streamlining the process. Or, better yet, why not just ship the thing preassembled?

A security bracket and cable tether are included so you can attach the Hyve to an immovable object on your property to prevent pirates from simply running off with the entire thing. (Unloaded, the device weighs 40 pounds. While awkward, it would be fairly easy to abscond with if it isn’t physically locked down.) Though oddly, the installation of these components is covered only in the video, not in the written instructions.

The unit is powered by four AA batteries and features a solar panel on top for trickle charging a backup battery. There’s also a USB-C port that can be used to supply emergency power if all else fails. Hyve says a fresh set of cells should last about five or six months, though strangely, my first quartet of AAs died inside of three weeks and without warning. There’s fortunately a USB-C port that can be used to supply emergency power if all else fails (which I needed when my cells died).

The Hyve Locker requires its own Wi-Fi bridge, which you must plug into an inside outlet near where you’ll be placing the locker. I found this to be a bit of a tall order, as I don’t have any power outlets in my entry hall, and an outlet only 15 feet away from the locker turned out to be out of range. (Exterior walls will do that to a wireless signal.) I ended up finding another outlet, forgotten in the guest room, that was able to reach the Hyve, but if that hadn’t worked, I would have been forced to relocate the locker elsewhere. Fortunately, the signal has held strong over several weeks of testing.

Hyve’s app is deceptively simple. At its most basic, the homeowner sets a master PIN, which everyone uses for access to the locker to both make deliveries and to retrieve them. It’s a simple idea, but it obviously presents a bit of a security risk, since anyone with the four-digit code can pop the lid open and rifle through what’s inside. Whether this is a legitimate concern or not is perhaps a matter of personal risk tolerance. Due to the physical design of the device, there’s nothing preventing one courier from removing a package that another has left inside the Hyve, but then again, there’s nothing preventing them from taking an unattended package off your doorstep, either. Presumably for Hyve, and I would agree, random passers-by are the bigger concern for most homeowners, so the monolithic PIN mode is probably good enough for many users.

If you want more fine-grained security than the mono-PIN, you’ll need a subscription plan. Hyve’s Essentials subscription plan runs $5 per month or $50 per year, the main feature being that you can set separate PINs for each delivery service or carrier (including major shippers as well as services including DoorDash, Instacart, Best Buy, and more). With this setup, the app notifies you each time the lid is opened, and it tells you who opened it (or at least who employs them), logging it in the system. One month of Essentials is included with purchase.

What do you do with all these PINs? Alas, you’ll have to go it alone, though Hyve provides detailed advice on how to enter the PIN and information about the lockbox into each carrier’s delivery instructions page on their website. You’ll need an account with each carrier, tied to your address, and I found that some of these instructions are more useful than others. Both FedEx and UPS, for example, provide fields for entering gate codes, but neither lets you specify specifically that packages should be left in a lockbox. (Both used to offer free-form delivery instruction fields, but these have recently changed into more simplified drop-down systems, and “lockbox” is not a choice for a delivery location.)

If you don’t have the Hyve Returns subscription but do have Essentials, you can still use the Hyve for on-demand returns by scheduling a pickup through Uber Courier, with no additional charges due to Hyve. The trick with this scheme is that while you avoid the $15 subscription fee, you have to pay Uber’s service charge for the pickup. Those fees vary based on the distance to your nearest UPS, FedEx, or Amazon drop-off location. For me, the Uber Courier charge for dropping off an Amazon return typically ranged from $8–18, making the $15 twice-monthly return plan far more enticing than the ad hoc option. (But alas, unavailable to me.)

I did test the alternate method by using Uber Courier to create a return, and found that Hyve didn’t add much to the equation. The only difference with Hyve is that instead of grabbing the item from the doorstep, the driver fetched it from the bin with a PIN. More secure? Yes, but given that I only had to wait 20 minutes for the driver to show up, the risk of an exposed package was minimal compared to receiving a delivery when I wasn’t home for days.

While the lockbox is rather obtrusive on my front porch, the hardware works well. The weatherproofing is fine, the door opens and closes with a satisfying, locking click, and the box sounds an alarm if it’s left open for too long. Push notifications from the Hyve mobile app come quickly and accurately, letting you know whether it was FedEx or Amazon—or you—that opened the hatch.

There is, unfortunately, a catch, and at first I found it to be an awfully big one. The problem was that no delivery driver seemed to want to use the Hyve locker, no matter how much I tried to get them to.

After getting everything set up on day one, I waited with anticipation when FedEx arrived with a box, and my phone lit up with a text from the company that the delivery had been completed. Alas, it was not in the Hyve locker but sitting next to it, nestled against the exterior. I was crestfallen, yet undeterred, and kept trying to get someone to open that hatch.

The next day, I encountered the FedEx driver in person, only because he rang the bell because he had a delivery with a signature required. I asked if he had seen the delivery instructions on my FedEx account and, with a puzzled look, said that he “thought he heard something” when pulling up to my house. It turns out that FedEx’s driver devices provide verbal instructions on where to leave packages (in addition to rather garbled written ones, which he showed me), but that he had the volume on his device turned down. Clad in my bathrobe, I demonstrated the Hyve to him personally and got his buy-in.

The following day, I was thrilled to get a push notification from the Hyve app that FedEx had successfully left a box for me inside. The driver even rang the bell again, only to show me his success with a smile. I tell you, opening that hatch and seeing my package inside was like Christmas morning for both of us.

Alas, on the third day, a fresh FedEx delivery appeared on the porch again. My driver had moved to another route.

I was about to give up on the whole shebang when, all of a sudden, something clicked. FedEx, UPS, and Amazon all started using the Hyve locker, and regularly. I soon became accustomed to getting notifications multiple times a day that the box had received a delivery, with my estimation of its usage rate approaching 75 percent. No longer was my doorstep darkened with cardboard, as trips to empty out the Hyve became an undertaking necessary to complete several times a day.

In fact, on some days, the usage level revealed an entirely new problem: A single UPS delivery of a few boxes could fill the locker, leaving no room for anything else. My hopes of leaving for a week and not having to worry about packages were dashed; there’s just not enough space for more than a day or two at most in the bin, given the pace of deliveries at my house.

Early on in my testing, I spoke to Hyve about the usage issues I was experiencing at the time, and its CEO freely admitted that this is, in no uncertain terms, a problem for many homeowners. To combat it, the company provides an adhesive sign that you can use to instruct carriers to use the box, and while this was likely quite helpful at improving usage rates, it’s not a panacea (nor is it particularly attractive).

And over a Zoom call, the CEO showed me another innovation that she said was having even better results: Attaching a placard that reads “Snack Stop” to the top of the lockbox, and stocking a collection of treats like chips and meat sticks inside for hungry drivers, encouraging them to open it up to grab a bite when making their rounds. What delivery driver could possibly say no to a free Slim Jim?

Nvidia has said it will invest $3 billion in Meta after the social media and AI giant announced plans to raise $95 billion to support its investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure.

Meta on Monday said it would initially raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, before raising an additional $60 billion with an at-the-market program.

The announcement said Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, and Broadcom were interested in purchasing up to $5 billion in shares.

Nvidia announced its investment on Tuesday, adding that Meta would expand Vera Rubin and Vera CPU deployment, and that the two companies would deepen their partnership on Muse, the social media giant's AI agent that launched last month.

"AI agents represent a new computing paradigm — software that understands our goals, reasons, uses tools and gets work done on our behalf," said Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in a statement.

"This changes how we use computers, from operating applications to working with intelligent agents."

"We're excited to keep working with NVIDIA to deliver the best personal agents and frontier models for billions of people," said Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

Both companies' shares were flat in premarket trading on Tuesday.

Nvidia has been rapidly building up stakes in companies powering the AI boom, investing in OpenAI, Anthropic, Intel and XAI.

The chip giant has participated in 121 investment rounds so far this year, according to Dealroom, up from just 13 in 2022.

#321. Just two drinks a day may be far riskier than you think

📅 25 October 2026 | Sumber

Even alcohol consumption that many Americans would describe as moderate may carry significant health risks, including a greater likelihood of premature death, disability, cancer, and heart disease. That is the conclusion of a new study published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, a journal published at Rutgers University.

The research, known as the Alcohol Intake and Health Study, was originally commissioned by the U.S. federal government to help shape updated national dietary recommendations. Researchers estimated that people who consume an average of 14 alcoholic drinks per week face a 1 in 25 lifetime risk of dying from alcohol-related causes. By comparison, consuming up to seven drinks weekly was linked to only small increases in risk for most health conditions.

"Even low levels of alcohol use come with health risks," says lead study author Kevin Shield, Ph.D., an associate professor at the University of Toronto and a senior scientist who leads the World Health Organization (WHO)/Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) Collaborating Centre in Addiction and Mental Health. "And that risk continues to increase the more someone drinks."

How Scientists Measured the Health Risks of Alcohol

To better understand the long-term consequences of drinking, Shield and his colleagues in the United States and Canada investigated how alcohol consumption over a lifetime contributes to disease and premature death among Americans.

Medical experts first examined more than 7,200 scientific publications covering illnesses and injuries associated with alcohol. Using this evidence, they estimated the risks for individual health conditions and combined those findings with large national health data sets. Statistical models then allowed the team to calculate how different levels of alcohol consumption affect the likelihood of developing serious health problems or dying prematurely.

The findings provide specific estimates that are missing from the latest U.S. Dietary Guidelines. The updated recommendations simply encourage Americans to "limit alcoholic beverages" without identifying a particular consumption threshold. Earlier versions advised men to drink no more than two alcoholic beverages per day and women no more than one.

"While the new U.S. Dietary Guidelines contain a useful 'less-is-best' message, they provide no quantitative framework. Our study was designed to do just that across the drinking spectrum," says study co-author Timothy Naimi, M.D., M.P.H., director of the University of Victoria's Canadian Institute for Substance Use Research and an adjunct professor at Boston University.

"It turns out that two drinks per day, which might be considered 'moderate' from a social standpoint, is associated with a substantially elevated risk of a premature death caused by alcohol," explains Naimi.

Moderate Drinking Offers No Significant Overall Health Benefits

The researchers looked beyond the risk of premature death to examine alcohol's connection to a wide range of immediate and long-term health problems. These included cancers (e.g., esophageal, oral, and breast), cardiovascular disease, liver disease, and injuries.

One of the study's most important findings challenges the longstanding belief that consuming small amounts of alcohol can improve health, particularly heart health.

"We did not observe a significant protective effect of alcohol on health at any level of consumption," says Shield. "At low levels, alcohol may be associated with a reduced risk of ischemic heart disease and stroke. But when you look across the full range of health outcomes, including cancer and other chronic diseases, those potential benefits are outweighed by the risks even at 7 drinks per week."

In other words, while some studies have suggested that light drinking may benefit certain aspects of cardiovascular health, those possible advantages do not translate into an overall health benefit once alcohol's links to cancer and other diseases are taken into account.

Although the analysis drew on extensive scientific evidence, the researchers emphasize that its estimates describe risks across populations rather than predicting precisely what will happen to any particular person.

Shield says the statistical calculations relied on "the best possible data." However, he cautions that individual circumstances can substantially influence the results.

"However, we can't assume that means one person's individual health risk is the same as what is reported here -- that depends on other factors like lifestyle, genetics, drinking patterns, and other choices that differ person to person."

To estimate alcohol's overall impact, the researchers calculated risks for health conditions already known to be caused by alcohol and combined them into a broader assessment. However, scientists are continuing to investigate additional possible consequences of drinking, including emerging evidence connecting alcohol consumption to pancreatic cancer.

"Understanding those relationships, and how much alcohol contributes to those risks, is an area that still needs further work," says Shield.

What the Findings Mean for U.S. Drinking Guidelines

The results suggest that alcohol-related health risks become more pronounced when consumption exceeds one drink per day, regardless of whether the person is male or female. This provides a more specific reference point for people trying to understand how their drinking habits might affect their long-term health.

Rather than suggesting that any particular amount is completely safe, the findings show how risks increase with greater consumption and why drinking less generally reduces exposure to alcohol-related harm.

"Having a clearer threshold helps people better understand what level of drinking is associated with increased risk and make more informed decisions when drinking," says Shield.

The study has also raised questions about how scientific evidence was incorporated into federal dietary recommendations.

In an accompanying editorial, Robert M. Vincent, a former Associate Administrator for the U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, offers his perspective on the circumstances surrounding the research and its role in the development of national guidance.

"The Alcohol Intake and Health report was explicitly invited to inform alcohol guidance during development of the Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2025-2030," he writes. "Despite the study's adherence to its mandate, its findings were sidelined."

Materials provided by Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#322. Amazon weighed ‘difficult trade-offs’ as memory costs squeezed its devices business, internal document shows

📅 27 October 2026 | Sumber

Amazon launched a flurry of new consumer devices this month. Behind the scenes, rising memory costs are adding pressure to its already money-losing hardware business.

An internal planning document obtained by Business Insider shows Amazon forecasting a $612 million gross loss this year for its first-party devices business, compared with a leadership target of a $438 million loss.

The document said rising memory costs were "putting pressure" on the business's profitability, forcing "difficult trade-offs" among sales volumes, average selling prices, and gross profit.

The projected $612 million loss was at the gross profit level, meaning it did not account for all operating expenses, such as R&D, sales and marketing, and administrative costs.

The figures offer a rare glimpse into the pressure on Amazon's hardware business as it absorbs rising component costs. Other tech hardware companies, including industry leader Apple, face similar pressure from surging memory chip prices.

An Amazon spokesperson declined to comment.

Despite the pressure, Amazon continues to expand its consumer hardware lineup. Even if the company loses money on device sales, it can make money in other ways, such as subscription services, as more customers use its gadgets.

In October alone, the company introduced new Kindles, Alexa-powered tablets, Ring smart locks, and AI wearables under its Bee brand. The August planning document identified Bee and new smart glasses as strategic products still in an investment phase.

Amazon has historically used low-cost hardware to pull customers into a broader ecosystem of shopping and digital content. Rising component costs could make that strategy more expensive, forcing the company to raise prices.

Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.

The clearest shift is in Amazon's tablets. Earlier this month, the company phased out Fire tablets after 15 years and replaced the budget-friendly lineup with pricier Alexa Tablets powered by Alexa+. The new devices cost between $229.99 and $499.99, a notable increase from previous generations.

The planning document was prepared in August, the same month Amazon raised prices on products including Echo speakers, Kindle e-readers, and Fire TV devices.

The pressure extends beyond Amazon. Apple has raised prices on some Macs and iPads, while Microsoft and Sony have increased console prices. Dell, HP, and Lenovo also face higher memory costs.

The AI boom is helping drive the squeeze. Huge data center investments have increased demand for memory chips, while manufacturers have devoted more capacity to high-bandwidth memory used in AI servers. That has tightened supplies and raised prices for components used across consumer electronics.

Amazon is experiencing both sides of the boom. It expects roughly $220 billion in capital expenditures this year, largely to expand AWS data centers for AI demand, while higher component costs squeeze its consumer hardware business.

The August planning materials show Amazon reassessing both Alexa+ revenue and operating costs. They called for updated forecasts, expansion through enterprise sales and advertising, and more detailed AWS cost modeling.

Amazon is now confronting the cost of operating Alexa+ at scale. Business Insider reported in July that internal forecasts put Alexa+'s AWS cloud costs at roughly $1.7 billion in 2026, nearly triple the prior year's figure. Amazon was working to lower those costs by relying less on Anthropic's AI models and routing more requests to its own, cheaper systems.

A separate project called Moonraker, intended to give Alexa more advanced AI-agent capabilities, was projected to require more than $100 million in GPU spending this year. Amazon internally considered delaying or scaling back the initiative as one option for easing cost pressure, Business Insider previously reported.

#325. What Can Magnus Norman Bring to Jannik Sinner?

📅 27 October 2026 | Sumber

Jannik Sinner has found his replacement for Darren Cahill, and it is a rather interesting choice. According to The Times, the Italian has selected Magnus Norman to join his coaching team in December, with the Swede working alongside Simone Vagnozzi from 2027.

Cahill, who helped transform Sinner into a five-time Grand Slam champion and World No. 1, is preparing to retire after extending his original coaching commitment by another season, and he's leaving enormous shoes to fill. Norman, however, is hardly an ordinary replacement.

The former World No. 2 helped Stan Wawrinka win three Grand Slam titles and guided Robin Soderling to consecutive Roland Garros finals. Both players became considerably more dangerous under his guidance, especially against opponents who had previously appeared almost unbeatable.

Which raises an intriguing question: What can Norman actually improve in a player who is already one of the best in the world?

There is an interesting similarity between Wawrinka and Soderling. Both possessed tremendous natural power, but neither initially appeared likely to become a multiple Grand Slam contender. Soderling was an aggressive baseliner who could hit through almost anyone when his game was working.

Under Norman, he became considerably more consistent, famously defeating Rafael Nadal at Roland Garros in 2009 before reaching the final. A year later, he defeated Roger Federer at the same tournament and reached another final.

Wawrinka's transformation was even more remarkable. When Norman began coaching him in 2013, the Swiss was already an established Top 20 player with an exceptional backhand. But he was not widely considered a genuine threat to Djokovic, Nadal and Federer at Grand Slams.

Within three years, he had won the Australian Open, Roland Garros and US Open so what changed? Well, Norman encouraged Wawrinka to trust his aggressive instincts, particularly on his forehand and serve, while improving his physical conditioning and tactical discipline.

That being said, Wawrinka did not suddenly become a fundamentally different player, he just became a more reliable version of the player he already was, and that's what matters in relation to Sinner. The Italian does not need somebody to teach him how to hit a tennis ball. His ability to take the ball early, generate extraordinary pace from both wings and consistently redirect shots is already among the best in tennis.

Trying to rebuild that foundation would make very little sense. What Norman could provide is another perspective on how to use those weapons, especially against opponents capable of matching his baseline intensity. Carlos Alcaraz is the obvious example.

When Carlos Alcaraz successfully disrupts Sinner's preferred rhythm through changes of pace, aggressive court positioning or unexpected approaches to the net, the Italian can occasionally become too dependent on his baseline patterns. Norman's work with Wawrinka suggests he might emphasize greater variety in how Sinner constructs attacking opportunities and that doesn't mean more power but simply more ways of creating situations in which that power becomes decisive.

Jannik Sinner of Italy plays a backhand against Benjamin Bonzi of France in the Men's Singles Round of 64 match during the Mutua Madrid Open 2026 tournament celebrated at La Caja Magica on April 24, 2026 in Madrid, Spain. Featuring: Jannik Sinner in action during the Mutua Madrid Open Day 4 at La Caja Magica on April 24, 2026 in Madrid Where: Madrid, Spain When: 24 Apr 2026 Credit: Oscar Gonzalez/WENN

Perhaps the most important consideration is that Norman is not replacing the entire coaching philosophy behind Sinner's success. After all, Vagnozzi is staying, and that makes the transition considerably less disruptive. During his partnership with Cahill, Vagnozzi has generally been responsible for much of Sinner's technical and tactical development, while the Australian provided experience, emotional guidance, and oversight of the broader team.

Their work on Sinner's serve is perhaps the clearest example of what that combination achieved. The Italian developed a more effective delivery, improved his ability to earn inexpensive points and became considerably more dangerous with his first shot after the serve.

Cahill also emphasized improving Sinner's movement and ability to transition from defense into offense. Norman's coaching background suggests a somewhat different emphasis. His greatest successes came with players who could produce extraordinary attacking tennis but needed greater consistency, physical resilience and confidence in the biggest matches.

Cahill, meanwhile, has demonstrated an exceptional ability to manage different personalities and playing styles, having previously worked with Lleyton Hewitt, Andre Agassi, and Simona Halep. Even so, it would be simplistic to describe Norman as the aggressive coach and Cahill as the tactical one.

Both understand those aspects of tennis. But Norman's experience developing Wawrinka and Soderling into players capable of defeating the sport's established giants could prove really useful.

There is also Roland Garros. Sinner has already won five Grand Slam titles, but the French Open remains missing from his collection. Norman reached the Roland Garros final himself in 2000, guided Soderling to two finals, and helped Wawrinka win the tournament in 2015.

None of that guarantees anything, but it gives him considerable experience preparing powerful baseline players for the physical and tactical demands of clay. And then there is Sinner's knee. The Italian has not competed since Wimbledon because of persistent knee problems, making his return to full fitness the immediate priority.

Norman cannot solve a medical problem through tactical adjustments. However, his experience managing Wawrinka's training and recovery later in the Swiss player's career could help the team make sensible decisions about workload once Sinner is cleared to compete.

Replacing Cahill was never going to be straightforward as he helped Sinner develop from an exceptionally promising player into one of the most dominant competitors in tennis. But Norman offers something valuable in his own right.

He has already demonstrated that he can help outstanding players become Grand Slam champions without fundamentally changing what makes them special. With Vagnozzi remaining in charge of much of the technical development, there is little reason to expect a dramatic reinvention of Sinner's tennis.

Instead, Norman's influence might be found in relatively small adjustments. Better decisions under pressure or greater attacking variety. We could also see a more effective preparation for difficult opponents. For a player already this good, though, those small improvements could make an enormous difference.

#326. What the US Movement Against Data Centers Can Learn From Abroad

📅 25 October 2026 | Sumber

Paris Marx’s new book couldn’t have landed at a better time. The longtime critic of Big Tech and host of the Tech Won’t Save Us podcast has been thinking about data centers for years, and Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech's Data Empires comes out right as opposition hits a fever pitch.

“I certainly didn't predict that it was all going to kind of come to a head as my book was coming out,” he says with a laugh.

While data centers are playing a role in shaping US elections—they’re one of the issues that could decide key midterm races in less than two weeks—there’s a history of struggle around the world. Marx’s book takes the reader on a tour of the tech industry’s quest for power and its opposition, from antiwar protests targeting American computers during the Vietnam War, to more recent resistance in Ireland and Chile, and an alternative vision for the future of data centers in New Zealand.

I caught up with him this week to talk about what he’s seen, and what could happen if the AI bubble pops.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

MOLLY TAFT: When did you decide to write a book about data centers?

PARIS MARX: In the Netherlands and Singapore, they had moratoriums going back to 2019. But in 2022, there was a growing recognition of the demands of data centers in Ireland, on the energy grid in particular. There were huge quantities of electricity that data centers were starting to consume over there.

The other story that really got on my radar was what happened with Google in The Dalles, Oregon. Google was really trying to hide its water use figures, to the degree that it got the city council to try to keep its water use figures secret. They kept that going for the better part of a year before the community finally got the actual numbers and found out that Google was using 29 percent of the water in the community.

ChatGPT came out at the end of 2022. It became apparent that there's going to need to be a lot more data centers for generative AI. These places were already feeling the effects of significant data center construction, and it felt like that was going to start coming to a lot more communities very soon.

I feel like a lot of Americans think data centers just came out of the blue in the US over the past year or two, just in time to be this huge midterms issue. One thing I like about your book is that it shows us how other countries and communities served as early warning signs.

Ireland was a real example of what can happen. Dublin had a moratorium passed back in 2021. It was actually the grid operator that said, “Hey, there are too many data centers. We do not have the grid capacity to connect any more of them.”

In response to that, you had the industry moving to make sure it can still build data centers in Ireland. They can't get grid connections in Dublin, so they start looking at building in other parts of Ireland. They also looked at starting to tap into the gas network so they can use generators. Eventually, they start building dedicated gas power plants to power their data centers instead of connecting to the grid.

The Irish energy grid is a public grid—only the public utility can build electricity lines. And data center companies actually lobbied for legislation that essentially allows private companies to build electricity cables. That obviously concerns a lot of people and presents questions about equity in the system.

The gas stuff looks so prescient with what’s happening in the US now, where companies are racing to build these massive private gas power plants for data centers.

[Data center operators] were getting these emission licenses from the Irish Environmental Protection Agency to be able to burn all these fossil fuels. The agency was warning that climate targets are going to be a lot harder to achieve now.

When I started to see that happen in the US, I wasn’t surprised. I’d already seen the story play out before. But the scale of it is staggering, and how quickly it’s escalated.

What happens to the physical infrastructure—from the gas plants to the data centers themselves—that's getting built out if this industry falls apart? Is there historic precedent for that?

I think we're in an AI bubble. But what does the collapse of that bubble look like? They're planning to add all these data centers and all of these gas power plants in order to power the data centers. But there are issues with getting turbines, with getting chips, with getting different kinds of pieces of the puzzle for the data center itself. Are these even going to get built out before there’s a reassessment of the demand for AI?

We often talk about the excess build-out of fiber capacity back in the dotcom boom and bust. But there was also a build-out of data centers—obviously a much earlier stage than what we're at now. A lot of data center companies went under. Companies like Equinix, which did survive, bought up a ton of data centers to be ready for when that capacity returned.

But the issue we have now is that if data centers are being planned for AI use, and we’re operating under the assumption that the chips are going to have to be cycled out within a few years. Even if the data center is there, what makes it most valuable is potentially not going to be useful by the time that demand returns.

Inevitably, even if the data centers don't come, then those gas plants will exist. They will be looking for new customers to justify their existence. I'm sure that people are not building them with the intention to just shut them down.

You ended the book with a specific example in New Zealand of a community-led effort to create a more accurate speech-recognition model of the Māori language, using local cloud providers to host the data. I really liked this alternative vision of a non-extractive way to harness the powers of AI. Have you thought about what we could do to make some changes and how this build-out is going?

I would like to see governments go really hard on actually putting firmer regulations on the development of data centers. But those should also be paired with regulations on the AI products themselves. We had a lot of promises about what generative AI was going to deliver that haven't been realized. There has also been a long list of harms that have arisen from these technologies that we were not told would come along with them. Our governments do not seem to be so willing to actually take that on. They're buying the narrative that generative AI is still what Sam Altman sold it to be in early 2023 rather than what it has become today.

I think that we do need to be thinking of how we do technology differently, especially in this moment where we're dedicating so many resources to the infrastructure to enable generative AI. We should be asking, how much computation do we really need? How many resources are actually justifiable to put into this project? What are we actually getting out of it, right?  Does what we're getting from what Silicon Valley is creating really justify the resources that we are collectively sacrificing in order to realize it? If we actually did the assessment, I think that we would very clearly find that there's no way to justify what we are doing right now—from a financial perspective, but also from a social and environmental one.

Speaking of those climate targets, it’s not just the Irish government that’s thinking about them. My colleague Joel Khalil covers how the European Union’s thirst for AI is running into European countries’ climate goals. Joel tells me he wouldn’t be surprised if data centers become a political flash point in Europe, like they are in the US, as countries go to the polls next year. “The fascinating thing about the European data center build-out is the collision of competing interests: national-level policy butts up against local priorities, ambitions for economic growth stand in conflict with climate objectives, and planning bureaucracy foils attempts by AI companies to rapidly expand their fleets,” he says. “It’s hard to see how Europe could possibly have it all.”

#327. Porsche profit rebounds as luxury carmaker reduces exposure to China

📅 27 October 2026 | Sumber

German sports carmaker Porsche said it has significantly reduced its exposure to China as operating profit rebounded in the first nine months of the year despite falling revenue and vehicle deliveries.

The Volkswagen-owned company published its third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, announcing that operating profit was 1.74 billion euros ($1.94 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, compared with 40 million euros at the same time last year, when it booked around 2.7 billion euros in strategic restructuring costs.

Meanwhile, sales revenue fell 5.9% to 25.28 billion euros, while deliveries continued to decline, down 16% to 178,532. North America remained Porsche's largest sales region by volume.

China has historically been an important market for German luxury automakers, but they have struggled with growing competition from domestic brands, particularly in electric vehicles.

Porsche's China sales have fallen sharply in recent years amid intensifying competition from brands such as BYD, Geely and Xiaomi.

"Our geographically balanced sales footprint continues to provide resilience across different markets," Jochen Breckner, Porsche's chief financial officer, said in the earnings webcast on Tuesday.

"As you know, we have significantly reduced our exposure to China. This makes our overall business less dependent on developments from this challenging market environment."

Porsche shares were last seen trading 2.3% higher.

Porsche is also cutting thousands of jobs as part of a broader restructuring aimed at reducing costs and responding to weaker demand.

Citi analysts said in a note Tuesday that Porsche's first-nine-month results were as expected, despite challenges including China.

"Despite challenging conditions, including exceptionally low deliveries, higher costs, and higher battery electric vehicle deliveries, Porsche's underlying EBIT remains very resilient and ahead of German premium peers," the analysts said.

They added that Porsche has laid out a plan to return to double-digit underlying operating profit margins, with recovery expected to start in 2028, and net cash flow expected to rebound to above its IPO levels by 2031.

"Whilst FY27 will remain a trough year, we still see a solid, well-supported and credible multi-year EBIT and net cash recovery starting financial year 2028 - unlike many peers," the analysts said.

#329. Labour faces accusations of breaking manifesto pledge over minimum wage for young people – UK politics live

📅 27 October 2026 | Sumber

Greens say Labour has ‘no respect for young people’ amid reports chancellor will pause equalisation of minimum wage for under-21s with that paid to older workers

Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, has not contested reports saying that, in the budget tomorrow, John Healey, the chancellor, will pause the process of equalising the lower national minimum wage paid to people under the age of 21 with the more generous national living wage that applies to older workers.

In an interview on the BBC this morning, Reynolds was asked to respond to a story suggesting the equalisation process has been put on hold because of concerns about youth unemployment.

In a story for the Times, Steven Swinford and Patrick Maguire report:

double quotation markJohn Healey will announce plans to increase the minimum wage by nearly 4% but slow the rise for young people after warnings that they are being priced out of jobs.

The Times has been told that the national living wage, which applies to those aged 21 and over, is expected to rise from £12.71 to around £13.20 – an increase of 3.9%.

However, Healey has decided not to repeat the big rises of the past two budgets in the national minimum wage, which applies to those aged 18 to 21. It will rise broadly in line with the rate for older workers – from £10.85 to around £11.27, an increase of 3.9%.

In its manifesto, Labour said it would raise the level of the national minimum wage to the level of the national living wage to “so all adults are entitled to the same minimum wage, delivering a pay rise to hundreds of thousands of workers across the UK”. The manifesto implied this would happen during this parliament, but in May Torsten Bell, the pensions minister, said implementation of this commitment could be delayed until after the general election – implying the government is worried equalisation now could increase youth unemployment.

Asked about the Times story on the Today programme, Reynolds insisted the new national living wage and national minimum wage rates would be announced tomorrow.

double quotation markThe manifesto pledge on equalisation still applies, but it was always clear it would happen over time and we would take into account, as the minimum wage uprating each year always does, the relative strength of the labour market and other pressures …

Of course, you want not just good wages, but good work. And the way this has always been done – it is a balance of making sure the pressures on the labour market are taken into account. That is the approach you will see confirmed [in the budget].

The Green party has accused Labour of breaking a manifesto promise. Responding to the Times’ story, and Reynolds’ comments in effect confirming it, Mothin Ali, the Greens’ co-deputy leader, said:

double quotation markAnyone doing a day’s work, needs to be paid the same rate for the same job. A young person’s rent and food bill is no less because they are young, so they need to receive the same wage.

Healey and Burnham are now breaking a manifesto pledge to young people that even Starmer managed to keep. Labour have no respect for young people, who appear to just be there for cheap labour for the wealthy and their corporate donors.

Ali said the Greens would introduce a £15 minimum wage for workers of all ages.

Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, has suggested that someone would not be banned from standing as a candidate for his party just for liking a social media post from the far-right activist and provocateur Tommy Robinson.

In his Today programme interview, Nick Robinson, the presenter, asked about the recent ITV News undercover exposé of Reform UK, which included footage of a potential candidate who flagged up pro-Robinson social media posts as a potential problem being told he should just delete his social media account.

Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, is currently on trial for harassment charges.

Asked if the ITV report showed that Reform UK’s vetting procedures were too lax, Farage said he “wouldn’t ban anybody for liking someone like Tommy Robinson”.

double quotation mark[It] wouldn’t be my cup of tea, but I wouldn’t ban anybody from doing so … I don’t want us to get into a world of cancel culture.

When Nick Robinson asked if Farage was saying it would be OK for a Reform UK candidate to approve any post by Tommy Robinson, Farage said that would depend what the post said. But he went on:

double quotation markI’m not going to have run a party where we say you can’t talk about that person or that person. We have to be sensible about vetting. And we are.

Farage also claimed that the BBC’s own experience with staff subsequently accused of paedophilia showed that all big organisations ran the risk of having rogue members or employees. And he claimed that Reform UK candidates were subject to a “much higher level” of scrutiny than candidates from other parties.

Referring to another person filmed in the exposé, a councillor with extreme racist views, Farage said that he was a former Conservative. When Nick Robinson put it to him that the ITV film suggested he had joined Reform UK because he realised he would be “among friends” there because other Reform UK members shared his views, Farage said that was “absolute cobblers”.

Back to “everyday fixes” (see 9.07am), and groups representing men have welcomed the news that self-employed men will be able to qualify for parental pay.

The Labour MP Amanda Martin, who co-chairs the Labour Men and Boys group, said:

double quotation markI’ve long believed that self-employed dads deserve the same chance as everyone else to be there for their families when a new baby arrives, so I’m delighted that this is becoming a reality. It’s about time self-employed fathers got the support they deserve.

Self-employed tradies build our homes, fix our heating and keep our lights on, so ensuring they can access paternity leave is a proper mark of respect for the people who keep our country going. This will make a real difference to tens of thousands of dads each year, giving them the chance to welcome their children into the world and be present fathers without facing financial ruin. I’m especially pleased that self-employed dads in my home city of Portsmouth will benefit.

And George Gabriel, co-founder of the Dad Shift, which campaigns for better paternity leave rights, said:

double quotation markPaternity leave is a cost of living lifeline for new families. This decision gives self-employed dads breathing space and a chance to show up for their loved ones when they’re needed the most.

The Women’s Budget Group, a feminist economic thinktank, has also welcomed the announcement. Eva Neitzert, its head of research and policy, said:

double quotation markWe’re pleased to see the chancellor recognise cost of living pressures on families and carers in his package of pre-announced measures. The lack of statutory paternity pay for self-employed fathers was a massive gap in parental leave …

We hope the chancellor will go further in his cost of living budget and increase statutory maternity pay as well. State support for new mum’s still sits at less than half of minimum wage beyond the first six weeks. Our cost benefit analysis of extending this to 12 weeks and raising pay to the national living wage found it was a net positive to the exchequer and would make the world of difference to families in the first nine months of their children’s lives.

Jakub Krupa writes the Guardian’s Europe live blog.

Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, has warned that Russia’s Vladimir Putin is “testing us and testing Nato’s resolve” as he condemned hybrid threats and “state-sponsored terrorism” from Russia.

Streeting repeated his recent warnings that “we have to be ready for a scenario in which the United Kingdom and the Nato alliance finds itself at war with Russia”. He went on:

double quotation markNot because we want war – we have no quarrel with the Russian people, and we have no desire for war with Russia; Nato is a defensive alliance – but when Putin gives assurances that he has no intentions to provoke a war with Nato, we are reminded of what he said about Ukraine only days before the invasion.

Speaking in Warsaw alongside Poland’s defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, Streeting stressed Nato is ready “to defend every inch of Nato territory” and will continue its support for Ukraine.

double quotation markThe more ready we are to face against Russia, to defend every inch of Nato territory, the less likely we are to find ourselves in that scenario.

Poland is one of our greatest and certainly our most reliable friend in Europe, and we value and treasure this friendship very much.

The partnership is “not simply about our shared history,” but also “our shared determination that in that contest between freedom and tyranny, the United Kingdom and Poland will not be bystanders.”

He said that UK forces will next month take part in major exercises as part of the multinational force for Ukraine.

Nigel Farage has rejected research showing that most of Reform UK’s donations have come from people or firms recently based overseas.

In a report for the Independent, Millie Cooke says:

double quotation markAn astonishing 80% of donations to Reform UK in the past 12 months have come from donors or companies recently based overseas, The Independent can reveal.

An analysis of data from the Electoral Commission shows the amount received from donors who were based abroad in the past two years by Nigel Farage’s party dwarfs that of other parties amid growing concern about overseas influence in British politics.

In comparison, Labour and the Conservatives received just 0.15% and 3.57% of their donations from people or companies based abroad respectively during the same period.

Asked about the Independent’s analysis in his Today programme interview, Farage said the conclusions were “completely wrong”.

double quotation markWhoever’s done this research doesn’t understand where people domicile, how they operate, where they live, and where they vote …

I can assure you, these people vote here, live here, some of them are international businessmen who travelled the world constantly. In the old days, we used to be proud of British pioneers that went out there and made a great success of their lives.

Asked why Reform UK was so reliant on donors who spent a lot of time abroad, Farage said it would be a lot easier for him if he could just “sell some peerages” like other parties.

(Of course, parties aren’t allowed to sell peerages. But Farage is right to say that donating large sums to a mainstream political party does seem to have a remarkably positive effect on one’s chance of getting a seat in the House of Lords.)

It is not just gherkins where the Treasury is cutting import tariffs. (See 9.07am.) Here is the lists from the Treasury of mostly food imports where tariffs are being cut.

double quotation markGarlic (8% + £100 per 100 kg)

Citrus jams, marmalades and pastes (20% + £19 per 100 kg)

Toffees, caramels and similar sweets (8%)

Plant-based beverages (soya, nut, cereal or seed) (8%)

The Treasury also cut tariffs on some food imports in the summer. It says “together, the two packages are expected to reduce consumer costs by approximately £245m to £595m a year”.

While this seems a big figure, the total amount Britons spend on food and drink a year is £300bn.

When Andy Burnham opened a debate on revising the Brexit settlement in his Labour conference speech, he did so on the basis of a simple proposition. He declared: “I cannot say to you truthfully that where we are is good enough. Brexit has done more harm than good.”

The Conservatives have strongly attacked Burnham’s move – but mostly on the basis that the 2016 referendum decision should be honoured, that a new debate would be divisive and that Burnham’s initiative went against assurances he made during the Makerfield byelection. Very few Tories have challenged the proposition that “Brexit has done more harm than good”, and Kemi Badenoch has not seriously tried to take on this argument.

Reform UK has also been keen to attack Burnham more on the basis of problems that rejoining the EU would throw up than on the basis of the supposed Brexit benefits the UK might be sacrificing. But, in an interview this morning on the Today programme, Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, did argue that Brexit had worked.

Asked if he regarded Brexit as a success, he replied:

double quotation markYes, I do. We certainly stand taller in the world. The terrible projections of doom as to what would happen to our financial sector etc haven’t happened. Our growth rates are higher than our European competitors. Our exports, particularly of services to the European Union, have actually rocketed. And we’ve now got more trade deals and more options around the rest of the world.

But Farage also accepted that Brexit had failed to cut immigration numbers in the way that people who voted for leave were expecting. “So yes, in the eyes of many, the delivery of Brexit has been a failure.”

Farage also claimed Burnham had no mandate to reopen the Brexit debate. He said:

double quotation markFive months ago, Andy Burnham says … I’m not going to reopen these arguments.

Two-and-a-half years ago, a Labour government got a massive majority in parliament saying we will not be re-entering the single market, the customs union, or opening up a debate on the free movement of people.

What I am saying is this: this prime minister has no mandate, and to hear that his officials are negotiating in Brussels already is really very, very poor indeed.

Unison has particularly welcomed the announcement today about higher tax-free mileage rates being made permanent. (See 9.07am.) The union has been campaigning for this, and some of its members will benefit.

But, in her response, Andrea Egan, Unison’s general secretary illustrated how there is a limit to how much goodwill a government can generate from small “everyday fixes”. She said:

double quotation markThese are welcome measures, especially making the uplift to mileage rates permanent, something Unison has campaigned hard for. The government’s relentless focus on the cost of living is commendable.

But the cost of essentials, including food and fuel, is going to keep soaring, meaning breathing space will quickly be closed down. That’s why we need to see a bolder approach, based on making the wealthy pay their fair share and improving the lives of working-class communities in a more enduring way.

The Treasury says three million people are expected to benefit from the mileage changes. It says:

double quotation markThese changes will provide £120 a year in additional tax savings for a worker doing 6,000 business miles, with someone driving 15,000 business miles receiving up to £300 in additional tax savings.

Good morning. Prime ministers tend to get judged by posterity by the decisions they take on the big issues of the day. But little things matter too in the here and now, often disproportionately, and Andy Burnham, more than his predecessors, has decided that what he calls “everyday fixes” are worth focusing on too. Alexandra Topping wrote a good analysis about the pluses and minuses of this approach last week. But she filed too soon, because this morning Burnham has announced another five.

These are all changes contained in tomorrow’s budget but being announced today – presumably because John Healey will have bigger surprises for MPs tomorrow, and the Treasury wants these measures to get some media attention today because tomorrow they will be overshadowed by another story.

One of the measures is of particular interest to the Guardian because we have highlighted the scandal that led to hundreds of thousands of people getting the carer’s allowance being ordered to pay back huge sums of money because inadvertently their weekly earnings went slightly above the threshold allowed. In other parts of the welfare system, people just have to return the overpayment, but the rules for carer’s allowance were draconian, and a tiny breach of the weekly earnings allowance could lead to people being ordered to pay back thousands of pounds.

As Patrick Butler and Pippa Crerar report in our splash, this rule is being scrapped.

But this is one of just five “everyday fixes” announced this morning. Here is what the Treasury says about them.

double quotation mark• Making higher tax-free mileage rates permanent and increasing support for nurses, care workers, self employed builders and others who drive for work. The chancellor is locking in the 55p per mile rate for the first 10,000 business miles and increasing the rate above 10,000 miles from 25p to 35p per mile, supporting around 3 million employees and self-employed people who use their own vehicle for work.

• Extending parental pay to more than 150,000 additional parents per year, including self-employed dads and partners who have previously missed out, giving eligible parents two weeks of support currently worth up to £194 a week so they can spend more time with their child.

• Ending the Carer’s Allowance cliff edge, so unpaid carers no longer lose their entire allowance simply for earning a penny over the Weekly Earnings Limit, equivalent to 16 hours of the National Living Wage. Instead, only £1 of support will taper away for every additional £1 earned.

• Removing import tariffs on more than 100 products, helping lower import costs on family favourites including baked beans, chocolate and gherkins, while also supporting farmers facing higher fertiliser bills and households that rely on kerosene heating oil. Together with tariff suspensions already introduced, households could save up to £21 on their food shop each year.

• Rolling out hundreds more Post Office drop boxes, bringing the total to 1,000, making it easier and more convenient for people to send and return parcels without having to queue at a Post Office counter, helping take some of the hassle out of everyday errands in the run-up to Christmas. This comes alongside upgrades to 600 Post Office branches by the end of the financial year, improving services for customers across the country.

There is more detail in the Treasury news release here.

It is always easy to mock, and the Conservatives could not resist. Here is their response, from Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor.

double quotation markRampant borrowing, soaring taxes and an utter inability to cut spending mean inflation has already wiped out the benefits of Burnham’s ‘everyday fixes’.

Shoppers face rising costs at the till and families are struggling to make ends meet, but Burnham’s plan is cheaper gherkins. This is an insult to families hammered by Labour’s tax rises.

The mention of gherkins in the Treasury press release did come as a surprise, given that they are not a key feature of the national diet, but maybe someone in Whitehall read the reports earlier this year about their importance for Pret a Manger sandwiches.

The problem with the Tory response is that, even though “everyday fixes” might not make a big difference, people tend to welcome them anyway. This is from Novara Media’s Aaron Bastani.

double quotation markPart of the genius with this stuff is the negative polarisation, when people start attacking perfectly sensible and helpful – albeit small – changes.

Actually I want longer Post Office queues please!

10.30am: Sarah Sackman, the courts minister, gives evidence to the Lords justice committee on support for jurors.

Morning: Andy Burnham hosts a meeting with Muslim leaders in No 10.

11.30am: Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, takes questions in the Commons.

Noon: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.

After 12.30pm: Dan Jarvis, the security minister, is expected to give a statement to MPs about the government’s ‘Be Ready’ resilience advice about stockpiling essentials.

#330. Scientists reveal the hidden danger of missing blood pressure medication

📅 25 October 2026 | Sumber

Missing doses of blood pressure medication could significantly reduce its ability to protect against heart attacks, strokes, and other serious cardiovascular problems, according to findings presented at ESC Congress 2026.

An estimated 1.4 billion adults worldwide between the ages of 30 and 79 have high blood pressure (hypertension), a major contributor to illness and death. Although medications that lower blood pressure are proven to reduce the risk of cardiovascular complications, approximately half of patients do not take their prescriptions as directed.

"We have evidence that poor adherence to antihypertensive medication is associated with worse outcomes," explained presenter, Miss Qianqian Yang from the University of Oxford, UK. "However, previous data has come from observational studies and could be confounded by other factors. We undertook an analysis of randomized trial data to assess the true impact of adherence on the benefits of antihypertensive treatment."

Major Study Examines the Impact of Missed Blood Pressure Medication

To better understand how consistently taking medication affects its benefits, researchers analyzed individual patient data from 91,339 participants across nine clinical trials. Each trial compared a blood pressure treatment (intervention group) with an alternative approach (comparator group: either placebo or a less-intensive regimen).

The researchers divided participants into two categories based on how closely they followed their prescribed treatment. Those who took at least 80% of their assigned medication were considered to have higher adherence, while those who took less than 80% were placed in the lower adherence group.

Even with the regular monitoring and structured conditions of clinical trials, patients became less consistent about taking their medication as time passed.

"A decline in adherence over time was apparent, even in the structured setting of trials," noted Miss Yang. Overall, 88% of participants met the higher adherence threshold during the first year, but that figure had dropped to just 79% by the fifth year.

Skipping Blood Pressure Pills Reduces Treatment Benefits

The difference in medication adherence was reflected in how much patients' blood pressure improved.

Among participants with higher adherence, systolic blood pressure, the top number in a blood pressure reading, was 5.2 mmHg lower in the intervention group than in the comparator group. For those with lower adherence, the difference was considerably smaller at just 3.0 mmHg.

Researchers then examined whether these differences translated into protection against major cardiovascular problems. The outcomes included strokes, heart attacks (myocardial infarction), ischemic heart disease, and heart failure that resulted in hospitalization or death.

The findings revealed a striking contrast. Among patients who consistently followed their treatment plans, the intervention group experienced an 11% lower incidence of major cardiovascular events compared with the comparator group. However, among patients with lower adherence, there was no statistically significant reduction in these events.

"Notably, our results reinforce the saying that 'drugs don't work in patients who don't take them.' Patients with lower adherence derived little or no cardiovascular benefit, whereas those with higher adherence had greater reductions in blood pressure and prevention of cardiovascular events," said Miss Yang.

Helping Patients Get Lifesaving Heart Protection

The researchers believe that helping people take their medication consistently should become a greater priority in the treatment of high blood pressure. They recommend more routine assessments of medication adherence, along with better patient education and practical strategies to make treatment easier to follow.

Possible approaches include simplifying medication schedules, combining multiple treatments into a single pill, and prescribing longer-acting drugs that can help limit the consequences of an occasional missed dose.

Professor Felix Mahfoud, Chair of the ESC Communication Committee, emphasized that missed medication has received too little attention as a contributor to poorly controlled blood pressure.

"For years, we have neglected non-adherence to medication as a cause for uncontrolled hypertension. Assessment of adherence should become a routine part of hypertension care so patients do not miss out on life-saving benefits. As healthcare providers, we are here to have open, non-judgmental conversations with our patients about any barriers they may have to taking medication, to help improve adherence."

Materials provided by European Society of Cardiology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
